question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
answer:
Yes — Avery shuffles, and Guile goes into Avery's library rather than staying in the graveyard.

Why: while turned face down by Ixidron, Guile is a 2/2 with no text, no name, and no abilities ([708.2b], [Ixidron ruling #4]), so as a 2/2 it takes 6 lethal combat damage from the 6/5 Jerrard of the Closed Fist and is put into Avery's graveyard. The moment Guile is in the graveyard it is a face-up card with its normal characteristics again, and its last ability ("When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library") is one that functions from the graveyard — it does not behave like a leaves-the-battlefield ability ([Guile ruling #5], [Guile ruling #0]). Losing the ability while on the battlefield doesn't stop the trigger; only losing it while in the graveyard (e.g., Yixlid Jailer) would ([Guile ruling #7]). Face-down status applies to the permanent on the battlefield, not to the card in the graveyard.

So the ability triggers, and on resolution Guile is shuffled into Avery's library. Note that the shuffle happens regardless of whether Guile is still there: if someone exiles Guile from the graveyard in response, Avery still shuffles the library, just without Guile in it ([701.24c], [Guile ruling #2]). The library is shuffled even if it contains zero or one cards ([701.24e]).

Number of players doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on how the defending player is chosen; the same result occurs in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.603.10: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

cited_text.708.2b: Face-down spells and face-down permanents have no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that allowed the spell or permanent to be face down. Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that object’s characteristics. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects,” and rule 707, “Copying Objects.”) A face-down permanent can’t be turned face down. If a spell or ability attempts to turn a face-down permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn’t change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.
cited_text.701.24c: Shuffle If an effect would cause a player to shuffle one or more specific objects into a library, that library is shuffled even if none of those objects are in the zone they’re expected to be in or an effect causes all of those objects to be moved to another zone or remain in their current zone. Guile says, in part, “When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner’s library.” It’s put into a graveyard and its ability triggers, then a player exiles it from that graveyard in response. When the ability resolves, the library is shuffled. Black Sun’s Zenith says, in part, “Shuffle Black Sun’s Zenith into its owner’s library.” Black Sun’s Zenith is in a graveyard, has gained flashback (due to Recoup, perhaps), and is cast from that graveyard. Black Sun’s Zenith will be exiled, and its owner’s library will be shuffled.
cited_text.701.24e: Shuffle If an effect causes a player to shuffle a library containing zero or one cards, abilities that trigger when a library is shuffled will still trigger.

answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
answer:
No. While The Scarab God is face down because of Ixidron, it has no abilities at all, so nothing about it can trigger from being blocked by Scathe Zombies — and in fact The Scarab God's printed abilities aren't blocked-related to begin with.

Why: creatures turned face down by Ixidron are 2/2 creatures with no text, no name, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost [Ixidron ruling #4]. "No text" means the face-down The Scarab God has no upkeep trigger ("each opponent loses X life and you scry X"), no {2}{U}{B} activated ability, and no death trigger while it stays face down. A triggered ability only exists to trigger if the object actually has it [603.2f], and triggers on blockers being declared happen at that point in the declare blockers step [509.1i, 509.3, 509.3c].

Also note that even face up, The Scarab God has nothing that triggers on becoming blocked, so Nia declaring Scathe Zombies as a blocker would not trigger it either way.

One consequence worth flagging: as a face-down 2/2, The Scarab God can die in combat to Scathe Zombies (2/2 trading with 2/2), and because the face-down permanent has no text, its "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step" ability isn't there to trigger.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming The Scarab God is still face down through the declare blockers step and combat damage. If something turned it face up before blockers were declared, it would have all its printed abilities again — but it still wouldn't have any ability that triggers on becoming blocked; only its dies-trigger would then apply if it died [The Scarab God ruling #1].

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count (the only multiplayer wrinkle in the rules provided concerns range of influence in limited-range games [801.7], which doesn't change the outcome since the relevant abilities simply don't exist while the creature is face down).

question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total are placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (assuming it had none beforehand), leaving it a 10/10.

Step by step:

1. Distribution: With only one target, all three +1/+1 counters from Biogenic Upgrade must go to Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (each target must get at least one counter, per [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #0]). Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own replacement text — "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead" — makes that 4 counters. Card text like this overrides the general expectation that exactly the stated number is placed.
2. Doubling: Doubling means putting on a number of counters equal to the number it already has ([701.10e], [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2]). It now has 4, so 4 counters would be put on it — and again Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability adds one, so 5 are actually put on.
3. Total placed: 4 + 5 = 9 counters. Since each +1/+1 counter adds +1/+1 in layer 7c ([122.1a], [613.4c]), the 1/1 Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 becomes 10/10.

Assumption on timing/state: this assumes Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 was already on the battlefield with zero +1/+1 counters when Biogenic Upgrade resolves. If it already had counters, add those to the pre-doubling total before doubling. If Alaia somehow controlled two copies of Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11, each would add one more counter per placement event ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #3]), and if other counter-modifying effects were present, Alaia chooses the order to apply them ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #1]).

Player count doesn't matter here: Biogenic Upgrade only targets creatures, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.

cited_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.
cited_text.122.1a: A counter is a marker placed on an object or player that modifies its characteristics and/or interacts with a rule, ability, or effect. Counters are not objects and have no characteristics. Notably, a counter is not a token, and a token is not a counter. Counters with the same name or description are interchangeable. A +X/+Y counter on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield, where X and Y are numbers, adds X to that object’s power and Y to that object’s toughness. Similarly, -X/-Y counters subtract from power and toughness. See rule 613.4c.
cited_text.613.4c: Within layer 7, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order. (See rule 613.7.) Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.) Layer 7c: Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness (but don’t set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value) are applied.

answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
answer:
Yes. The copies made by Elemental Eruption's storm ability will each have Everdream's text spliced onto them, so each copy creates a 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess and then draws you a card.

Why: splice lets you reveal a card from hand and pay its splice cost ({2}{U} for Everdream) as you cast an instant or sorcery, adding that card's rules text to the spell ([Splice], [702.47c], [612.10]). That's a choice made while casting Elemental Eruption. Copying a spell copies its characteristics and all decisions made for it ([707.10]), and Everdream's own ruling states this directly: if a spell is copied, the copy will have the same abilities spliced onto it as the original ([Everdream ruling #4]).

Details worth noting:
- Storm reads "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" ([702.40a]). Ferocious Zheng was cast earlier this turn, so with just that one prior spell you get 1 copy (plus the original Elemental Eruption). Any other spells cast earlier in the turn by any player each add a copy too ([Elemental Eruption ruling #1]).
- The storm copies are put directly onto the stack and are not cast ([707.10], [Elemental Eruption ruling #2]). Splice normally requires casting a spell, but you don't re-splice here — the spliced text simply comes along as part of the copied spell's text.
- The spliced Everdream effect happens after Elemental Eruption's own effect ([702.47b], [Everdream ruling #1]), so each copy makes the token, then draws.
- Neither Elemental Eruption nor Everdream targets, so there are no target-legality problems ([702.47d]).
- Everdream stays in your hand as a revealed card — it's never put on the stack — and if Elemental Eruption itself is countered, Everdream remains in hand ([Everdream ruling #0]) and the copies are unaffected ([Elemental Eruption ruling #0]).

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the only difference is that in multiplayer, more spells cast earlier in the turn by any player mean more storm copies, each carrying the spliced Everdream text.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
gold_text.702.47a: Splice Splice is a static ability that functions while a card is in your hand. “Splice onto [quality] [cost]” means “You may reveal this card from your hand as you cast a [quality] spell. If you do, that spell gains the text of this card’s rules text and you pay [cost] as an additional cost to cast that spell.” Paying a card’s splice cost follows the rules for paying additional costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h. Since the card with splice remains in the player’s hand, it can later be cast normally or spliced onto another spell. It can even be discarded to pay a “discard a card” cost of the spell it’s spliced onto.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.

cited_text.Splice: Splice. A keyword ability that lets a player add a card’s rules text onto another spell. See rule 702.47, “Splice.”
cited_text.702.47b: Splice You can’t choose to use a splice ability if you can’t make the required choices (targets, etc.) for that card’s rules text. You can’t splice any one card onto the same spell more than once. If you’re splicing more than one card onto a spell, reveal them all at once and choose the order in which their effects will happen. The effects of the main spell must happen first.
cited_text.702.47c: Splice The spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards. This is a text-changing effect (see rule 612, “Text-Changing Effects”). The spell doesn’t gain any other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, supertypes, card types, subtypes, etc.) of the spliced cards. Text gained by the spell that refers to a card by name refers to the spell on the stack, not the card from which the text was copied. Glacial Ray is a red card with splice onto Arcane that reads, “Glacial Ray deals 2 damage to any target.” Suppose Glacial Ray is spliced onto Reach Through Mists, a blue spell. The spell is still blue, and Reach Through Mists deals the damage. This means that the ability can target a creature with protection from red and deal 2 damage to that creature.
cited_text.702.47d: Splice Choose targets for the added text normally (see rule 601.2c). Note that a spell with one or more targets won’t resolve if all of its targets are illegal on resolution.
cited_text.612.10: A splice ability changes a spell’s text by adding the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, following that spell’s own rules text. It doesn’t modify or replace any of that spell’s own text. (See rule 702.47, “Splice.”)
cited_text.702.40a: Storm Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. “Storm” means “When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.”
cited_text.707.10: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, “Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.” Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets. Fling is an instant that reads, “As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature” and “Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature’s power to any target.” When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling. Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, “You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.” Because mana isn’t an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion won’t cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.

answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
answer:
Torsten Von Ursus survives. Because Nova's Felidar Umbra grants umbra armor — "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a] — Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 ability does not destroy Torsten Von Ursus. Instead, all damage marked on Torsten Von Ursus is removed and Felidar Umbra is destroyed. Torsten Von Ursus stays on the battlefield under Nova's control, and Allen gets nothing from that target (no card was put into a graveyard from Torsten Von Ursus, so there is nothing of Torsten Von Ursus to return under Allen's control).

Details:
- Umbra armor's replacement is mandatory, not optional, and it applies whether the destruction comes from lethal damage or from an effect that says "destroy" — Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 is the latter [Felidar Umbra ruling #3][Felidar Umbra ruling #5].
- Umbra armor is not regeneration: Torsten Von Ursus does not become tapped and is not removed from combat, and "can't be regenerated" clauses wouldn't stop it [Felidar Umbra ruling #6].
- Per [Felidar Umbra ruling #7], when a spell or ability says it would "destroy" the enchanted creature, that spell or ability is what destroys the Aura instead — so it is Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability that destroys Felidar Umbra. That arguably makes Felidar Umbra a card "put into a graveyard this way," which Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability tells Allen to return to the battlefield under his control. The rules provided here don't cover how an Aura entering the battlefield without being cast chooses (or fails to find) a permanent to enchant, so I can't settle that last step from this context.
- Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 can hit up to three targets; if Nova had multiple umbra-armor Auras on Torsten Von Ursus, only one would be destroyed, and Nova chooses which [Felidar Umbra ruling #2]. Felidar Umbra also can't save two creatures destroyed simultaneously [Felidar Umbra ruling #1].

Nothing here depends on the player count: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since the ability simply targets and returns cards under its controller's (Allen's) control.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.303.4f: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.
gold_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”

cited_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”

question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
answer:
No. Alma has already used their one land play for the turn on Dryad Arbor, so Alma can't also play Sequestered Stash (absent an effect granting an additional land play).

Why: Dryad Arbor is both a land and a creature, and an object that's both a land and another card type can only be played as a land, never cast as a spell [305.9] [300.2a], and playing Dryad Arbor "counts as your land play for the turn" [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]. Playing a land is a special action that doesn't use the stack — the player simply puts the land onto the battlefield [305.1] [701.18a]. That action was taken and completed, so the land play is spent.

Because Dryad Arbor was played rather than cast, Nico's Containment Priest sees a nontoken creature entering the battlefield that wasn't cast and exiles it instead [Containment Priest ruling #1 confirms only cast creatures are spared]. The exile changes nothing about the land drop: to see whether another land can be played you compare the number of lands Alma may play this turn with the number already played this turn, including lands played as special actions [305.2a], and Alma can't play a land if that number is equal to or less than the number already played [305.2b]. One played, one allowed — so Sequestered Stash stays in hand.

Timing note: I'm assuming Containment Priest was already on the battlefield when Alma took the land-play special action (Nico could also flash it in earlier, but not in response to the land play itself, since a land play can't be responded to [305.1]). Either way the result is the same. If Alma had some effect letting them play an additional land this turn, Sequestered Stash could then be played during a main phase with an empty stack while Alma has priority [505.6b].

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since the land-play limit is per player per turn.

A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. See rule 305, “Lands.”

question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
answer:
Ari gets Marit Lage — and to be transparent about grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not cover this interaction (they concern cleanup, ending the turn/combat phase, look-back-in-time triggers, the world rule, etc.). My answer rests entirely on the provided card rulings for Blood Sun and Dark Depths, which are authoritative and directly settle each step.

1. Blood Sun says all lands lose all abilities except mana abilities. Dark Depths' "enters with ten ice counters on it" modifies how it enters, and Blood Sun strips such an ability before it applies, so Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters [Blood Sun ruling #5]. Dark Depths has no mana ability to keep [Dark Depths ruling #0], and its sacrifice/Marit Lage ability is suppressed too, so nothing triggers while Blood Sun is out.

2. Ari casts Sultai Charm choosing "Destroy target artifact or enchantment," a legal target since Blood Sun is an enchantment, and destroys Blood Sun.

3. With Blood Sun gone, its ability-removing effect no longer applies and Dark Depths has its abilities again [Blood Sun ruling #4]. Dark Depths does not re-enter the battlefield, so it does not gain ten ice counters now — it still has zero.

4. Dark Depths' last ability is a state trigger, so it triggers as soon as the condition (no ice counters on Dark Depths) is met and the ability isn't already on the stack [Dark Depths ruling #1]. On resolution Ari sacrifices Dark Depths and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible.

Caveats: if Dark Depths leaves the battlefield before that trigger resolves, Ari can't sacrifice it and gets no token [Dark Depths ruling #2]; if the trigger is countered while Dark Depths is still there with no ice counters, it triggers again immediately [Dark Depths ruling #1]. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and multiplayer.

Such effects may come from the permanent itself if they affect only that permanent (as opposed to a general subset of permanents that includes it). They may also come from other sources. To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account replacement effects that have already modified how it enters the battlefield (see rule 616.1), continuous effects from the permanent’s own static abilities that would apply to it once it’s on the battlefield, and continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent. Voice of All says “As this creature enters, choose a color” and “This creature has protection from the chosen color.” An effect creates a token that’s a copy of Voice of All. As that token is created, the token’s controller chooses a color for it. Yixlid Jailer says “Cards in graveyards lose all abilities.” Scarwood Treefolk says “This creature enters tapped.” A Scarwood Treefolk that’s put onto the battlefield from a graveyard enters the battlefield tapped. Orb of Dreams is an artifact that says “Permanents enter tapped.” It won’t affect itself, so Orb of Dreams enters the battlefield untapped.

answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with Mistform Skyreaver's mana cost {5}{U}{U}, plus "{2}: Discard a card.").

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability is a text-changing effect, not a copy effect, and it gives Volrath's Shapeshifter "the full text" of the top creature card of your graveyard — name, mana cost, color, types, abilities, power, and toughness [612.6] [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5] [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," which strips abilities from the Mistform Skyreaver card while it sits in the graveyard, but it does not change or blank that card's text. Volrath's Shapeshifter reads that text and gains flying on the battlefield, where Yixlid Jailer's effect doesn't reach (Yixlid Jailer only affects cards in graveyards). Compare Yixlid Jailer ruling #1, where a changeling card in a graveyard still has all creature types, and Yixlid Jailer ruling #3, where "as this enters"/enters-with abilities still apply once the card is on the battlefield — Yixlid Jailer's reach is limited to the graveyard itself.

Flying means a creature can't be blocked except by creatures with flying and/or reach, and a creature with flying can block creatures with or without flying [702.9a] [702.9b] [702.17b]. So Volrath's Shapeshifter, while Mistform Skyreaver is on top of Aiden's graveyard, is a 6/6 flier that can only be blocked by fliers or creatures with reach. It also keeps Mistform Skyreaver's "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn" ability, and no "enters" abilities trigger from the form change [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4].

Note: if the top card of Aiden's graveyard stops being a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 blue creature with just "{2}: Discard a card" and loses flying [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0]. This all works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
answer:
No — Autumn does not create a Zombie token.

Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are put into Autumn's graveyard at the same moment. Bridge from Below's first ability ("Whenever a nontoken creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield, if this card is in your graveyard...") is a leaves-the-battlefield-style trigger, so the game "looks back in time" to the moment immediately before the event to see whether the ability existed and whether its condition was met [603.10a]. Immediately before Silvercoat Lion died, Bridge from Below was on the battlefield, not in the graveyard — and while Bridge from Below is on the battlefield it does nothing at all [Bridge from Below ruling #1]. Per [Bridge from Below ruling #0], if Bridge from Below isn't in your graveyard immediately before a creature dies, its abilities won't trigger at all. So there is no trigger and no token is created [701.7a].

Had Bridge from Below already been in Autumn's graveyard before Hour of Revelation resolved, Silvercoat Lion's death would have triggered it and Autumn would create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token (provided Bridge from Below is still in the graveyard as the ability resolves).

On cost: unless there were ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield when Autumn began casting it, Hour of Revelation cost {3}{W}{W}{W}; with ten or more, the {3} generic is reduced away and it costs just {W}{W}{W} — the three white symbols are never reduced [Hour of Revelation ruling #0].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more: Bridge from Below's abilities care only about which graveyard cards are put into, not who controlled them [Bridge from Below ruling #3]. In a multiplayer game, opponents' creatures dying to Hour of Revelation would go to their own graveyards, which is Bridge from Below's second (exile) ability — but again only if Bridge from Below was already in a graveyard beforehand. If both a creature of yours and an opponent's creature died while Bridge from Below was in your graveyard, you'd choose the order of the two triggers and could make the token before exiling Bridge from Below [Bridge from Below ruling #2].

question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
answer:
Axl simply doesn't draw a card, and doesn't get anything from outside the game either — the draw step's draw is replaced by an effect that does nothing.

Ring of Ma'rûf's ability creates a replacement effect: "The next time you would draw a card this turn, instead put a card you own from outside the game into your hand." "Outside the game" means anything not in one of the game's zones — typically your sideboard or personal collection; it is not a zone itself [400.11c]. If Axl owns no such cards, there is nothing to put into hand.

The key point is that draw-replacement effects still apply even when the replacement can't actually produce a card — the rules say such effects are applied even if no cards could be drawn [121.6a] [614.11]. So during Axl's draw step, the turn-based draw [504.1] is replaced rather than performed: Axl ends up with no card. The replacement is consumed ("the next time"), so a later draw that turn would work normally.

Axl does not lose the game from this. Losing for drawing from an empty library only happens when a player actually attempts to draw from a library with no cards [121.4] [704.5b]; here no draw attempt occurs at all, because it was replaced.

Timing note: I'm assuming the ability resolved during the upkeep step, before the draw step, so the replacement effect was in place when the draw would happen. Also note that if for some reason Axl would draw no cards at all during the rest of the turn, the ability likewise does nothing [Ring of Ma'rûf ruling #0].

This answer is the same whether there are two players or more — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

cited_text.704.5b: The state-based actions are as follows: If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game.

Cards outside the game can’t be affected by spells or abilities, except for characteristic-defining abilities printed on them (see rule 604.3) and spells and abilities that allow those cards to be brought into the game.

answer_gold: Axl is required to attempt to find a card from outside the game, if they fail to find one, then when the ability resolves they will put nothing into their hand. Since Ring of Ma'rûf sets up a replacement effect, Axl can't choose to ignore it.

question: Athena control [Krark, the Thumbless] and [Spark Double] copying it. They cast [Song of Totentanz], which triggers both Krark, the Thumbless. When the first trigger resolves they lose the flip and return Song of Totentanz to hand. What happens when the second trigger resolves?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): when the second Krark, the Thumbless trigger resolves, Athena still flips a coin. If Athena loses that flip, nothing happens, because Song of Totentanz is no longer on the stack and nothing is returned [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #4]. If Athena wins that flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is still created on the stack even though the original spell is gone [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #12], with the same value of X chosen as Song of Totentanz was cast [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #3]; the copy is created rather than cast, so no cast triggers fire off it [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #2].

To be transparent about grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me address a spell leaving the stack before a linked "whenever you cast" trigger resolves, so this answer rests entirely on the provided Krark, the Thumbless card rulings (which are authoritative on their own), plus Spark Double's own text making the copy non-legendary [Spark Double ruling #6] so Athena has two Krark abilities, and Song of Totentanz's ruling that only creatures controlled as it resolves gain haste [Song of Totentanz ruling #0]. I am not citing any numbered rule for the core interaction because the provided rules text does not cover it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. answer_gold: If Athena loses the flip, nothing happens. If Athena wins the flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is created.

question: Alden cast [Ixidron]. Natalie controls a very cute [Tangled Florahedron]. What happens to it?
answer:
Direct answer: Natalie's Tangled Florahedron (on the battlefield with its front, creature face up) is a nontoken creature, so Ixidron's enter-the-battlefield replacement effect turns it face down as Ixidron enters. As a face-down permanent it becomes a nameless 2/2 creature with no text, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost — meaning it loses "{T}: Add {G}" and can no longer tap for green mana [Ixidron ruling #4].

Timing details: the turning face down happens *as* Ixidron enters, not after, so there is never a moment when Ixidron is on the battlefield and Tangled Florahedron is face up; "whenever another creature enters" abilities on Tangled Florahedron (it has none) wouldn't see Ixidron anyway [Ixidron ruling #3]. This is a replacement effect modifying how Ixidron enters, and characteristics are checked as the permanent would exist on the battlefield [614.12]. If instead Tangled Florahedron were entering the battlefield simultaneously with Ixidron, it would enter face up [Ixidron ruling #1]. If Natalie had already played the back face, Tangled Vale, it's a land and not a creature, so Ixidron wouldn't touch it.

Ixidron's own power and toughness will count every face-down creature on the battlefield, so the face-down Tangled Florahedron adds to Ixidron's size.

One gap, stated plainly: the rules excerpts provided here don't include any rule about whether a modal double-faced card such as Tangled Florahedron // Tangled Vale may be turned face down at all (the provided ruling only says it can't be *transformed*). If such a restriction exists, Tangled Florahedron would simply stay face up; I can't confirm that from the context given.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players — Ixidron says "all other nontoken creatures," so in a multiplayer game every other player's nontoken creatures are turned face down too, not just Natalie's.

question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
answer:
Loxodon Smiter ends up on the battlefield, at Nicolas's choice. Both Leyline of the Void and Loxodon Smiter are replacement effects trying to replace the same event — "Loxodon Smiter is put into Nicolas's graveyard." Leyline of the Void says to exile it instead; Loxodon Smiter says "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard," and Hypnotic Cloud is a spell Amani (an opponent) controls, so its condition is met.

When multiple replacement effects would apply to the same event, the affected object's controller/owner chooses which one to apply — the same principle shown in the melded-permanent example, where a player affected by both Leyline of the Void and Wheel of Sun and Moon chooses one effect to apply [712.21d]. Here the affected card is Nicolas's, so Nicolas chooses. If Nicolas applies Loxodon Smiter's own text, the card goes from his hand to the battlefield and never would be put into a graveyard, so Leyline of the Void's exile replacement has nothing left to replace and does not apply. Loxodon Smiter's printed text is what beats the general graveyard-bound outcome here.

Either way, the card was still discarded, so "whenever a player discards" triggers still trigger [Loxodon Smiter ruling #0], [Leyline of the Void ruling #2]. Note that Loxodon Smiter would enter the battlefield under Nicolas's control, since he's the player putting it there [110.2a].

If Nicolas instead chose Leyline of the Void's effect, Loxodon Smiter would be exiled and abilities checking the discarded card could still find it in exile [Leyline of the Void ruling #2] — but a player will normally pick the battlefield.

This works identically with two players or more than two; Hypnotic Cloud targets a single player, and Leyline of the Void applies to each of Amani's opponents' cards.

question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
answer:
Short answer: No for Parhelion II (as long as another player is legally attackable), and yes for the Angel tokens.

**Parhelion II.** Kardur, Doomscourge's ability applies to creatures your opponents control for the duration of the effect, including permanents that become creatures under an opponent's control after the ability resolved — the ability isn't locked to only the creatures present on resolution [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #2]. Once Bode crews Parhelion II, it is an artifact creature Bode controls, so it "attacks each combat if able and attacks a player other than you if able." In a 4-player Commander game all three opponents are within Bode's range of influence and may be attacked [801.3], so Bode has legal attack targets other than Ari and must send Parhelion II at one of them (or at a planeswalker/battle of theirs, per Bode's choice) [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #3]. Bode could only attack Ari with Parhelion II if no other player (or opposing planeswalker) could legally be attacked [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0]. Also note the requirement is only "if able" — if Parhelion II is never crewed it isn't a creature and simply doesn't attack at all [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #4], [302.5].

**The Angel tokens.** Yes, they can be attacking Ari. When Parhelion II attacks, its triggered ability creates two 4/4 Angels that are put onto the battlefield already attacking; Bode chooses which defending player, planeswalker, or battle each one is attacking, and they need not match Parhelion II's target [Parhelion II ruling #0], [508.4a]. Those tokens are "attacking" but were never declared as attackers and, for triggers and effects, never "attacked" [Parhelion II ruling #1], [508.4a]. Kardur, Doomscourge's requirement is a restriction/requirement on the declaration of attackers [508.1b], so it doesn't govern creatures that are merely placed into combat by an effect — Bode may point both Angels at Ari.

**Two players vs. multiplayer:** in a two-player game Kardur, Doomscourge's "attack a player other than you" clause would have no other player available, so Parhelion II could attack Ari (or an Ari-controlled planeswalker) [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0], [506.2]. In this 4-player game the other opponents exist, so the redirection bites.

**Assumption on timing:** I'm assuming Parhelion II is crewed during Bode's turn while Kardur, Doomscourge's "until your next turn" effect is still active (Bode's turn comes before Ari's next turn). If Bode's combat happened after Ari's next turn began, the effect would have ended and Bode could freely attack Ari with Parhelion II.

Oxidda Finisher is unaffected by this analysis beyond being a creature Bode controls, which likewise must attack a player other than Ari if able.

Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

question: Aislinn controls two [Bramblewood Paragon]s and casts [Thunder-Thrash Elder]. What is the maximum amount of counters Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Thunder-Thrash Elder enters with 8 +1/+1 counters, assuming Aislinn's only other creatures are the two Bramblewood Paragons: 6 from devouring both Bramblewood Paragons (devour 3 × 2 creatures sacrificed) plus 2 more from the two Bramblewood Paragons' replacement effects.

Details:
- Thunder-Thrash Elder is a Lizard Warrior, so each Bramblewood Paragon's "Each other Warrior creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it" applies, and the effects of multiple Bramblewood Paragons are cumulative — two of them mean two extra counters [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #1] [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #2].
- Devour 3 lets Aislinn sacrifice any number of creatures already on the battlefield as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters; it can't devour itself or anything entering with it [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #0]. Both Bramblewood Paragons are already on the battlefield, so both can be devoured: 2 × 3 = 6 counters. Choices for devour are made as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #1], and both the devour replacement effect and the Bramblewood Paragon replacement effects modify that single entering event, so all of them apply and the total is 6 + 2 = 8. Each object can only be chosen to change zones once across these entering-replacement effects [614.13b], which isn't a problem here since only devour moves anything.
- If Aislinn controls other creatures beyond the two Bramblewood Paragons, the maximum is 3 per creature sacrificed plus 2, so with N total sacrificeable creatures it's 3N + 2.
- The counters exist as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield with them [122.6a].

This is a player-count-neutral answer: nothing here depends on how many opponents are at the table, and it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games. Note also that whose graveyard/zone a Warrior came from is irrelevant to Bramblewood Paragon [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #3].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1c: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects.

cited_text.614.13b: An effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield may cause other objects to change zones. The same object can’t be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield. Jund (a plane card) says, “Whenever a player casts a black, red, or green creature spell, it gains devour 5.” A player controls Runeclaw Bear and casts Thunder-Thrash Elder, a red creature spell with devour 3. As Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, its controller can choose to sacrifice Runeclaw Bear when applying the devour 3 effect or when applying the devour 5 effect, but not both. Thunder-Thrash Elder will enter the battlefield with zero, three, or five +1/+1 counters, depending on this choice.
cited_text.122.6a: Some spells and abilities refer to counters being put on an object. This refers to putting counters on that object while it’s on the battlefield and also to an object that’s given counters as it enters the battlefield. If an object enters the battlefield with counters on it, the effect causing the object to be given counters may specify which player puts those counters on it. If the effect doesn’t specify a player, the object’s controller puts those counters on it.

answer_gold: Eight. Both Bramblewood Paragon and Thunder-Thrash Elder have replacement effects that modify how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield. While Thunder-Thrash Elder is entering the battlefield the game checks which replacement effects to apply, and sees that there are two Bramblewood Paragons that want to place an additional +1/+1 counter on Thunder-Thrash Elder as well as a Devour ability. If Aislinn chooses to devour the Bramblewood Paragons, they will place an additional six +1/+1 counters on Thunder-Thrash Elder.

question: Is [Umori, the Collector] a legal companion for a deck containing only [Grist, the Hunger Tide], creatures, and lands?
answer:
Yes. With Grist, the Hunger Tide as the only planeswalker-ish card, Umori, the Collector is still a legal companion, because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card everywhere except the battlefield.

Why:
- Umori, the Collector's companion condition requires that there be one card type every nonland card in your starting deck has [Umori, the Collector ruling #1]. Creature is that shared type here.
- Grist, the Hunger Tide's own text says "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," and the ruling confirms that anywhere but the battlefield Grist, the Hunger Tide is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3]. Card text like this overrides the general expectation that a planeswalker card is only a planeswalker. Deck construction happens outside the battlefield, so Grist, the Hunger Tide counts as a creature card there [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #2].
- Land cards are exempt from the condition, and they may have any extra types [Umori, the Collector ruling #4].
- Note Grist, the Hunger Tide is also a planeswalker card, but that doesn't matter: the condition only asks that *some* one type be shared by all nonland cards, not that they share every type.

In Commander specifically: you may have one companion, your deck including your commander must meet the condition, and the companion isn't one of your 100 cards [Umori, the Collector ruling #7]. The companion is set aside before you set aside your commander [702.139b]. Umori, the Collector's color identity is black-green, so its color identity must fit inside your commander's color identity [903.11a]; with Grist, the Hunger Tide (black-green) as commander that's fine, and it can't share a name with a card in your starting deck [903.11a].

Before the game, you reveal Umori, the Collector from outside the game [103.2b, 702.139a, Umori, the Collector ruling #8]. Later, once during the game, at a time you could cast a sorcery (main phase, stack empty, you have priority), you may pay {3} — three generic mana — as a special action to put it into your hand [702.139a, Umori, the Collector ruling #9].

Multiplayer note: in a table of more than two players, if several players want to reveal companions, the starting player reveals first and the rest follow in turn order [Umori, the Collector ruling #2]; the legality analysis above is unchanged at any player count.

question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
answer:
After Mirrorweave resolves, Abel's Adrestia is a nonlegendary land named Mobilized District with mana cost of nothing (a land has no mana cost), no subtypes other than none printed (just "Land"), and only Mobilized District's printed abilities: "{T}: Add {C}" and "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." It loses islandwalk, the attack-trigger Assassin ability, crew 1, its legendary supertype, its Artifact/Vehicle types, and its 4/3 power and toughness.

Why: Mirrorweave affects "each other creature," and Adrestia was a creature because Abel crewed it, so it is affected (only the target, Mobilized District, must be nonlegendary). A copy effect copies only copiable values — the values from printed text as modified by other copy effects — not type-changing effects, counters, or status [707.2, 707.2a, 613.2a, 613.1a]. Mobilized District was animated by its own activated ability, which is a type-changing effect, not a copiable one, so that animation is NOT copied [Mirrorweave ruling #0, Mirrorweave ruling #5]. That's exactly the animated-Mutavault example: the other creatures become unanimated copies.

One important consequence: the crew effect that turned Adrestia into an artifact creature is a noncopy effect and keeps applying in the type-changing layer [Mirrorweave ruling #2], so Adrestia is still a creature — but nothing sets its power and toughness anymore, since Mobilized District's printed text gives none. As a 0/0 creature it will be put into its owner's graveyard the next time state-based actions are checked (Adrestia's controller can avoid this only by giving it toughness). If your table instead reads the crew animation as fully overwritten, Adrestia would simply be a noncreature land named Mobilized District and survive; either way it no longer has islandwalk, crew, or its Assassin trigger.

Timing assumption: Mirrorweave was cast and resolved after Mobilized District's animation resolved and while Adrestia was still crewed. If Adrestia's crew had already worn off (it wasn't a creature), Mirrorweave wouldn't affect Adrestia at all.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — Mirrorweave hits each other creature on the battlefield regardless of controller.

question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
answer:
No — Jasmine Boreal stays in exile.

Moonmist says "Transform all Humans," and Lunarch Inquisitors is a Human Cleric on the battlefield, so it transforms back to its front face, Avacynian Missionaries. But transforming isn't leaving the battlefield. The exile effect lasts "until this creature leaves the battlefield," and the ruling for this card states explicitly that if Lunarch Inquisitors somehow transforms into Avacynian Missionaries, the exiled creature remains exiled; it returns only if Avacynian Missionaries later actually leaves the battlefield [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #5]. That return is a second one-shot effect created immediately after the specified event (the permanent leaving the battlefield), returning Jasmine Boreal to the battlefield under its owner's control [610.3c].

A couple of side points:
- Jasmine Boreal is itself a Human, but Moonmist only transforms Humans on the battlefield, and Jasmine Boreal is in the exile zone, so it's untouched. Even on the battlefield it couldn't transform, since it isn't a double-faced card or token [712.9], as Moonmist's own reminder text notes.
- Any Equipment that was attached to Avacynian Missionaries remains attached through the transform [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #1].
- Multiplayer note: if Ari (Lunarch Inquisitors's owner) leaves the game, the exiled Jasmine Boreal does return, because the returning one-shot effect isn't an ability on the stack [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #3]. That's the only multiplayer-specific difference here; in a two-player game the answer is otherwise the same.

question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
answer:
Bioessence Hydra triggers exactly once, and that single trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

Why: Carth the Lion says "Planeswalkers' loyalty abilities you activate cost an additional [+1] to activate," so the [+1] cost of Dovin, Architect of Law becomes [+2] ([Carth the Lion ruling #3]). The total cost is calculated first, and the counters are then added all at one time as a single payment — you do not add one, then another ([Carth the Lion ruling #0], [606.5]).

Bioessence Hydra's ability reads "Whenever one or more loyalty counters are put on planeswalkers you control, put that many +1/+1 counters on this creature." Because both loyalty counters go onto Dovin, Architect of Law simultaneously as one event, that's one trigger for "one or more," and "that many" is 2 — so Bioessence Hydra gets two +1/+1 counters from one trigger.

This is independent of player count: it works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since only Addison's own permanents are involved.

Side note on a related case: if Addison controlled two copies of Carth the Lion, the cost increase would be cumulative for a total of [+3] here ([Carth the Lion ruling #1]), still a single payment and thus still one Bioessence Hydra trigger, but for three +1/+1 counters.

question: Nico casts [Assert Authority] targeting Ainsley's [Blightsteel Colossus]. What happens as Assert Authority resolves?
answer:
Assert Authority counters Ainsley's Blightsteel Colossus spell and exiles it — Blightsteel Colossus's "shuffle it into its owner's library instead" ability does not apply, because that ability only replaces an event that would put Blightsteel Colossus into a graveyard, and Assert Authority's own text already sends it to exile rather than to the graveyard.

Assumption on timing/target: Assert Authority says "Counter target spell," so this only works while Blightsteel Colossus is still a spell on the stack (Ainsley has cast it and it hasn't resolved). If Blightsteel Colossus were already a permanent on the battlefield, Assert Authority would have no legal target at all and would be countered on resolution for having an illegal target.

Why the shuffle doesn't happen: per rule 608.2c, later text on a card can modify the meaning of earlier text — you read the whole text of Assert Authority together, so the countered spell's destination is exile, not the graveyard. Because Blightsteel Colossus is never put into a graveyard, the condition of its replacement effect ("If Blightsteel Colossus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere...") is never met, so there's no competing replacement effect for Ainsley to choose between under rule 616.1f. Blightsteel Colossus simply ends up in the exile zone, out of Ainsley's library.

Mana cost note: Assert Authority costs {5}{U}{U}, and its affinity for artifacts reduces only the generic portion — {5} — by {1} for each artifact Nico controls. The two {U} symbols must always be paid with blue mana; with five or more artifacts Nico pays just {U}{U}.

This analysis is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; countering a spell and exiling it doesn't depend on the number of players.

question: Amani has 3 life. Briar casts [Chain of Plasma], targeting Amani. As it resolves, Amani pays the cost to copy it, and chooses to have the copy target Campbell. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Chain of Plasma deals 3 damage to Amani, dropping Amani from 3 life to 0. Amani may still discard a card and make the copy — that all happens during Chain of Plasma's resolution, before any player gets priority and before state-based actions are checked — so a copy of Chain of Plasma, controlled by Amani, goes on the stack targeting Campbell. Once Chain of Plasma finishes resolving, Amani loses the game for having 0 life.

Details:

1. Chain of Plasma's own text sequences the events: damage first, then "that player ... may discard a card. If the player does, they may copy this spell and may choose a new target for that copy." Amani is the damaged player, so Amani is the one who may discard and copy. Nothing about being at 0 life stops Amani from taking that action mid-resolution.

2. The copy is put onto the stack rather than cast, and it is controlled and owned by the player under whose control it was put there — Amani (707.10). It copies all the decisions made for the original except the target Amani changes.

3. Changing the target to Campbell is fine as long as Campbell is a legal target for "any target"; only the final set of targets is evaluated for legality (115.7e, 707.10c). If the copy resolves, it deals 3 damage to Campbell, and then Campbell in turn may discard a card to copy it again and possibly pick a new target.

4. Multiplayer note: the question involves three players, so this is a multiplayer game, and "any target" lets Amani point the copy at any legal target in the game, including Briar or Campbell or a creature/planeswalker/battle. The card's redirection of the copy privilege to the damaged player works the same regardless of player count.

What the provided rules don't settle: I can't tell you from the rules given here what happens to Amani's copy of Chain of Plasma still sitting on the stack once Amani leaves the game — the context contains no rule about objects owned or controlled by a player who leaves the game (the only related snippet, 614.9, just says a damage-redirection effect does nothing if it would redirect to or from a player who has left the game). Check the rules on a player leaving the game for that piece.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming Amani was at 3 life when the damage was dealt, i.e., the lethal damage and the copy decision both happen inside the same resolution of Chain of Plasma. If instead Amani had already been reduced to 0 or less and had left the game before Chain of Plasma resolved, there would be no player to discard and no copy at all.

question: In a multiplayer game, Achilles uses [Jon Irenicus, Shattered One] to give [Vastwood Gorger] to Brynn. If Brynn dies, what happens to Vastwood Gorger?
answer:
Vastwood Gorger goes back to Achilles' control and stays on the battlefield. Achilles still owns Vastwood Gorger — Jon Irenicus, Shattered One only granted Brynn control of it, not ownership. When Brynn leaves the game, all objects owned by Brynn leave the game, and "any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end" [800.4a]. So Jon Irenicus, Shattered One's control-change effect ends and Vastwood Gorger reverts to its owner and default controller, Achilles.

Notes:
- Vastwood Gorger keeps the +1/+1 counters that were put on it, and it remains goaded for the rest of the game and keeps "This creature can't be sacrificed" [Jon Irenicus, Shattered One ruling #0] — though goad only matters while an opponent controls it, so under Achilles' own control it no longer forces attacks.
- Vastwood Gorger is not exiled. Exile under [800.4a] only applies to objects still controlled by the departing player after control effects end, and [800.4c] only exiles an object when the player who controlled it by default (its owner, Achilles) is the one who left. Here Achilles is still in the game.
- If instead Achilles had left the game, Vastwood Gorger — owned by Achilles — would leave the game with him [800.4a].
- This scenario is inherently multiplayer: in a two-player game, one player leaving ends the game rather than continuing it [800.4a].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading "Brynn dies" as Brynn losing and leaving the game while Vastwood Gorger is on the battlefield under Brynn's control. If Vastwood Gorger had already left the battlefield (e.g., died to combat damage, i.e. put into a graveyard from the battlefield [700.4]), it would already be in Achilles' graveyard, since an object going to a graveyard other than its owner's goes to its owner's graveyard instead [400.3].

question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
answer:
The myriad tokens stay on the battlefield — they are not exiled. Time Stop ends the turn, and per Time Stop's own text and rule 724.1d the current phase/step ends, all attacking and blocking creatures (including the Hammers of Moradin tokens) are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every intervening step. Since abilities that trigger "at end of combat" trigger as the end of combat step begins (511.2), and that step never happens, the myriad delayed triggered ability from Hammers of Moradin ("If one or more tokens are created this way, exile the tokens at end of combat," rule 702.116a) never triggers, so nothing exiles the tokens. They remain permanently as ordinary creature tokens you control.

Details and timing: I'm assuming the tokens were already created (the myriad trigger resolved when Hammers of Moradin attacked) and Time Stop resolved later, during the combat damage step, as stated. Any triggered abilities still waiting to go on the stack when the end-the-turn process starts simply cease to exist (724.1a); no player gets priority during the process (724.1f). During the cleanup step, all damage is removed from permanents and all "until end of turn" / "this turn" effects end (514.2, 703.4p). If instead Time Stop had resolved before the myriad trigger resolved, that myriad trigger would have ceased to exist and no tokens would have been created at all.

Note also that the end step is skipped, so "at the beginning of the end step" abilities don't trigger this turn (724.1e, Time Stop ruling #1).

Player count: this only matters for how many tokens exist in the first place — myriad makes a token for each opponent other than the defending player, so in a two-player game Hammers of Moradin makes no tokens at all (Hammers of Moradin ruling #3) and the question is moot; with three or more players there is at least one token, and each such token survives the ended turn.

question: If Avery is going first, they'd like to reveal [Umori, the Collector] as their companion. If they're going second, they don't want to have a companion. Can they do this?
answer:
Yes. Revealing a companion happens after the starting player has been determined, so Avery already knows whether they're going first or second when they make that choice, and they can decide accordingly.

Details:
- Rule 103.2b places the companion reveal among the additional steps taken *after* the starting player has been determined. So the turn order is settled information at that point.
- Companion is a keyword ability that works from outside the game: before the game begins, you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition your starting deck fulfills, and it stays outside the game until you pay {3} to put it into your hand ([702.139a], [702.139c]). Umori, the Collector's condition is "Each nonland card in your starting deck shares a card type," so Avery's deck must satisfy that to reveal it at all ([Umori, the Collector ruling #1], [Umori, the Collector ruling #8]).
- Order of reveals: the starting player reveals first, then the remaining players in turn order, and once a player declines they can't change their mind ([Umori, the Collector ruling #2], and the general APNAP-style ordering in [101.4b]). So if Avery is going first, Avery declares Umori, the Collector before opponents declare; if Avery is going second (or later), they simply decline when their turn to declare comes.
- This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the only difference is that with more than two players, more opponents declare after the starting player, in turn order.

One caveat: the decision is made once, at that step. Avery can't reveal Umori, the Collector and then "take it back" later; the choice is locked in when made.

question: Aspen casts [Greater Good] sacrificing their [Bane Alley Blackguard] which is enchanted with [Mystic Subdual]. How many cards do they draw?
answer:
Aspen draws zero cards, then discards three cards.

Bane Alley Blackguard is a 1/3. Mystic Subdual gives the enchanted creature -2/-0, so Bane Alley Blackguard's power on the battlefield was 1 - 2 = -1. Greater Good's ability uses the sacrificed creature's power as it last existed on the battlefield ([Greater Good ruling #0]), so the draw instruction is "draw -1 cards." Magic only uses integers and can't draw a negative number of cards; an effect that attempts something impossible does as much as possible [609.3], so no cards are drawn (effectively zero) [107.1c].

The rest of Greater Good's ability still happens: Aspen then discards three cards, all while the ability resolves, with no chance for anyone to act in between ([Greater Good ruling #2]). If Aspen has fewer than three cards in hand, they discard their whole hand ([Greater Good ruling #1]).

Note that Mystic Subdual also makes Bane Alley Blackguard lose all abilities, but that doesn't matter here since Greater Good's sacrifice ability belongs to Greater Good, not to Bane Alley Blackguard. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
