question: Ari controls [Mana Reflection] and [Looming Spires]. Nicole controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ari taps the Looming Spires for mana, how much mana is produced, and of what type(s)?
answer:
Ari ends up with a single {C} (one colorless mana) — no red mana at all.

Why: "Tapping a permanent for mana" means activating a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its cost, and the replacement effects modify the mana-production event as that ability resolves and produces mana [106.12b], [Mana Reflection ruling #3]. Looming Spires' ability would normally produce {R}. Two replacement effects want to modify that event, so Ari (the controller of the affected mana ability) picks the order, and each effect can apply only once [Damping Sphere ruling #2].

- Mana Reflection applies: Looming Spires produces twice as much of that mana, i.e. {R}{R}.
- Now Looming Spires (a land) has been tapped for two or more mana, so Damping Sphere applies: it "produces {C} instead of any other type and amount" — that replaces both the type and the amount, leaving exactly one {C}.

If Ari tries to apply Damping Sphere first, it isn't applicable yet (only one mana would be produced), so Mana Reflection applies and makes it two mana; Damping Sphere, which hasn't yet applied to this event, then becomes applicable and still reduces the result to one {C} [Damping Sphere ruling #2]. Either way the answer is one {C}.

Note that Damping Sphere's text overrides the general expectation that Mana Reflection's doubling sticks — the card explicitly replaces both type and amount. Also, Mana Reflection itself produces no mana; it only modifies what Looming Spires produces [Mana Reflection ruling #2]. Even with several Mana Reflections (cumulative doubling, [Mana Reflection ruling #1]), Damping Sphere would still cut it to one {C}.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count: Damping Sphere's first ability affects any land tapped for two or more mana regardless of who controls it, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.5: A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event. A player controls two permanents, each with an ability that reads “If a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage to that permanent or player instead.” A creature that normally deals 2 damage will deal 8 damage—not just 4, and not an infinite amount.

cited_text.106.12b: To “tap [a permanent] for mana” is to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost. See rule 605, “Mana Abilities.” A replacement effect that applies if a permanent “is tapped for mana” or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.

answer_gold: {C}. As the ability resolves, Mana Reflection replaces "Add {R}" with "Add {R}{R}". Damping Sphere then applies and replaces that with "Add {C}". Mana Reflection won't apply again.

question: Natasha and Nico are playing Two-Headed Giant, and each controls their own copy of [Bloodbond Vampire]. Ariel controls [Wall of Shards], and on their next upkeep they put the third age counter on it. Can Ariel have Natasha gain one life and Nico gain two? If so, how many triggered abilities of Bloodbond Vampire will be put on the stack?
answer:
Yes, Ariel can do that, and three Bloodbond Vampire triggers go on the stack — one from Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire and two from Nico's Bloodbond Vampire.

Why Ariel can split it: Wall of Shards has "Cumulative upkeep—An opponent gains 1 life," and with the third age counter on it Ariel must pay that cost three times (once per age counter) or sacrifice Wall of Shards; partial payment isn't allowed [Wall of Shards ruling #1]. Ariel may choose a different opponent for each age counter, or the same opponent more than once [Wall of Shards ruling #0]. So "Natasha gains 1, Nico gains 1, Nico gains 1" is a legal payment.

Why three triggers: Bloodbond Vampire reads "Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature," and it triggers once per life-gaining event [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #0]. In Two-Headed Giant, life gained by your teammate does not trigger your own Bloodbond Vampire, even though the team's shared life total goes up [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #1]; damage, life loss, and life gain happen to each player individually and only the result is applied to the team's shared life total [810.9, Shared Life Total]. So:
- Natasha's 1 life gain: triggers Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire once (not Nico's).
- Nico's two separate 1-life gains: these are two separate life-gaining events (compare [702.15e], where multiple lifelink sources cause separate life gain events and trigger such an ability twice), so Nico's Bloodbond Vampire triggers twice (not Natasha's).

Total: 3 triggered abilities, each putting one +1/+1 counter on its own Bloodbond Vampire. Note that if your table instead treated Nico's two increments as a single lumped life-gain event, Nico's Bloodbond Vampire would trigger only once, for 2 total — but the per-payment reading above matches how separate life-gain events are handled in [702.15e] and [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #2].

Also note this Two-Headed Giant answer is about a shared team life total; larger teams (Three-Headed Giant, etc.) work the same way with higher starting life [810.11], and Ariel could spread the three payments among any opponents, including more than one member of the opposing team.

question: Nataly controls [Urza's Saga] with 2 lore counters on it. Alex casts [Magus of the Moon]. What does Urza's Saga look like?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes an Enchantment Land — Saga Mountain whose only ability is "{T}: Add {R}" — and then Nataly immediately sacrifices it as a state-based action.

Details:

- Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Urza's Saga is a nonbasic land, so it loses its other land types (Urza's) and all of its abilities, gaining the Mountain land type and "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4]. That includes losing its chapter I, II, and III chapter abilities, and also losing the mana ability and Construct-token ability it had gained from chapters I and II (those are abilities of the permanent, and Magus of the Moon strips abilities) [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], [Urza's Saga ruling #5].
- Magus of the Moon only changes land types; it doesn't remove the enchantment type or the Saga enchantment subtype, and it doesn't change names or supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1]. So Urza's Saga is still a Saga with no chapter abilities.
- A Saga with no chapter abilities is sacrificed immediately as a state-based action, which doesn't use the stack [Urza's Saga ruling #1], [704.5s], [714.4]. The 2 lore counters are irrelevant; the sacrifice happens because there are no chapter abilities at all, not because of the counter count.

Timing assumption: Magus of the Moon's static ability only applies once Magus of the Moon is on the battlefield, so nothing happens while the spell is merely on the stack. As soon as Magus of the Moon resolves and enters the battlefield, the layer change and then the sacrifice happen — the next time any player would receive priority. If Magus of the Moon is countered or otherwise never enters the battlefield, Urza's Saga is unaffected and continues to gain a lore counter in Nataly's precombat main phase [505.4], [714.3c].

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, including those controlled by every other player, so every player's Sagas that are also nonbasic lands are sacrificed by their own controllers.

question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
Ornithopter of Paradise survives, and it ends up tapped with no damage marked on it.

Step by step, assuming Metallurgeon's ability resolves first (it was activated in response, so it's on top of the stack and resolves before Prismari Command): Ornithopter of Paradise gets a regeneration shield — a replacement effect that will replace the next destruction event affecting it by instead tapping it, removing all damage marked on it, and removing it from combat (rule 701.8c: "A regeneration effect replaces a destruction event").

Then Prismari Command resolves. Its controller follows its instructions in the order written (608.2c), so the "deals 2 damage" mode happens first: 2 damage is marked on Ornithopter of Paradise, which is lethal for a 0/2. Then the "destroy target artifact" mode tries to destroy Ornithopter of Paradise, and the regeneration shield is used up to replace that destruction — Ornithopter of Paradise becomes tapped and all damage marked on it is removed.

Crucially, the lethal-damage destruction is a state-based action that is only checked when a player would receive priority, which is after Prismari Command has finished resolving. By that time the marked damage is already gone, so no second destruction occurs and Ornithopter of Paradise stays on the battlefield. Niko can no longer tap it for mana this turn since it's tapped.

If you instead assume Prismari Command somehow resolved before Metallurgeon's ability (not possible here, since Metallurgeon's ability was activated in response and resolves first), Ornithopter of Paradise would be destroyed with no shield in place, and Metallurgeon's ability would have no legal target on resolution.

Note also that only one regeneration shield exists, so it absorbs only the one destruction event. Metallurgeon's ability can target Ornithopter of Paradise because Ornithopter of Paradise is an artifact creature, and per Metallurgeon ruling #0 a colored/colorless distinction doesn't change that it interacts normally as an artifact. This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players at the table.

When Prismari Command resolves, the game carries out the instructions in the order written. First, Prismari Command deals 2 damage to Ornithopter of Paradise. The replacement effect generated by the regeneration ability will not apply yet, as even though Ornithopter of Paradise has been dealt lethal damage, it would only be destroyed when state-based actions are checked, and state-based actions are checked when a player would get priority. Next Prismari Command tries to destroy Ornithopter of Paradise and the replacement effect applies, replacing the destruction event with Ornithopter of Paradise being tapped and having all damaged marked on it removed. Lastly Prismari Command finishes resolving and leaves the stack and state-based actions are checked. Since Ornithopter of Paradise no longer has any damage marked on it, it will not be die.

question: Ahmed controls [Bronze Sable]. They cast [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Solemnity] onto the battlefield. Does Bronze Sable get a phylactery counter?
answer:
No — Bronze Sable does not get a phylactery counter, and Phylactery Lich will be sacrificed.

Why: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Solemnity onto the battlefield at the same time, so Solemnity is already on the battlefield when Phylactery Lich's replacement ability ("As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control") is applied [Genesis Wave ruling #5]. Bronze Sable is a legal choice, since it's an artifact that was already on the battlefield rather than one entering alongside Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #1], and the choice doesn't target and can't be interrupted [Phylactery Lich ruling #3].

But Solemnity says "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands," and that applies both to counters put on a permanent as it enters and to counters put on it later [Solemnity ruling #8]. The narrow exception in [Solemnity ruling #6] only covers a permanent that would *enter the battlefield with counters on it* simultaneously with Solemnity; Bronze Sable is not entering — it's an artifact already on the battlefield — so that exception doesn't help. Also, Solemnity's card text overrides the general counter-placement rule for putting counters on permanents on the battlefield [122.6a].

Result: Ahmed chooses Bronze Sable, but zero phylactery counters are actually placed. Since Ahmed then controls no permanents with phylactery counters on them, Phylactery Lich's last ability — a state trigger — triggers immediately and Ahmed must sacrifice Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #0], [Phylactery Lich ruling #2]. (If it were somehow countered while the condition remained true, it would just trigger again.)

This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.17a: Some effects state that something can’t happen. These effects aren’t replacement effects, but follow similar rules. “Can’t” effects must exist before the appropriate event occurs—they can’t “go back in time” and change something that’s already happened.

cited_text.122.6a: Some spells and abilities refer to counters being put on an object. This refers to putting counters on that object while it’s on the battlefield and also to an object that’s given counters as it enters the battlefield. If an object enters the battlefield with counters on it, the effect causing the object to be given counters may specify which player puts those counters on it. If the effect doesn’t specify a player, the object’s controller puts those counters on it.

answer_gold: Yes. Phylactery Lich and Solemnity enter the battlefield at the same time. Solemnity's effect must exist before Phylactery Lich enters the battlefield in order to prevent Bronze Sable from getting a counter.

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
Short answer: No phylactery counter gets put anywhere at all — because Humility enters at the same time as Phylactery Lich and strips Phylactery Lich of its "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" ability, so there is no counter-placing effect to apply. (Ironically, Humility also strips Tatterkite of "This creature can't have counters put on it," so Tatterkite would have been a legal choice if the ability still existed.)

Why:

1. All the permanents from Genesis Wave enter the battlefield simultaneously [Genesis Wave ruling #5]. So Humility is already on the battlefield as Phylactery Lich arrives.

2. Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" is a continuous effect applied in layer 6, the ability-removing layer [613.1f], and it removes every creature ability, including mana abilities [Humility ruling #1]. Phylactery Lich is a creature, so as it enters it has no abilities — neither the "as this creature enters" counter ability nor the "when you control no permanents with phylactery counters" state trigger. That state trigger being gone also means Phylactery Lich won't be sacrificed for lacking a phylactery counter (contrast [Phylactery Lich ruling #0], which assumes the ability is intact).

3. Tatterkite: its ability normally stops any kind of counter, not just -1/-1 counters [Tatterkite ruling #1], and it functions as the object enters as well as on the battlefield [113.6i]; an effect that would put a counter on it simply doesn't affect it [Tatterkite ruling #2]. But Tatterkite is a creature, so Humility removes that ability too in layer 6 [613.1f]. Note that Humility grants nothing and removes rather than prevents, so this is ability removal, not a "can't" effect fight [101.2a].

Timing/ordering note: I'm assuming Humility and Phylactery Lich truly enter together off the same Genesis Wave resolution, which is what Genesis Wave does. If instead Humility were already on the battlefield first, the result is identical. If Phylactery Lich somehow entered while Humility was not yet on the battlefield, its as-enters ability would work and you could put the phylactery counter on Tatterkite only if Tatterkite's ability were already removed; otherwise Tatterkite would be an illegal home for the counter and no counter would be placed [Tatterkite ruling #2]. Also, Tatterkite is fine as a choice on the "already on the battlefield" requirement — you may not choose an artifact entering simultaneously with Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #1], and Tatterkite was already there.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on opponents' choices.

cited_text.613.1f: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can’t have an ability are applied.
cited_text.113.6i: Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows: An object’s ability that states counters can’t be put on that object functions as that object is entering the battlefield in addition to functioning while that object is on the battlefield.
cited_text.101.2a: When a rule or effect allows or directs something to happen, and another effect states that it can’t happen, the “can’t” effect takes precedence. Adding abilities to objects and removing abilities from objects don’t fall under this rule. (See rule 113.10.)

answer_gold: No. Phylactery Lich and Humility enter the battlefield at the same time. Tatterkite had the ability that prevents it from getting counters immediately before Phylactery Lich entered the battlefield, which is when it matters.

question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
answer:
Direct answer: At the start of Avery's next turn, the Teferi's Protection effects end (Avery's life total can change again and the protection from everything from Teferi's Protection expires), and then, before Avery untaps during the untap step, the first The One Ring and every other permanent that phased out phases in — still indestructible and still with whatever burden counters it had. Because both copies of The One Ring are then on the battlefield under Avery's control at the same time, Avery must keep one and put the other into the graveyard; indestructible does not help against that, since it isn't destruction. Then, in the upkeep step, each The One Ring still on the battlefield triggers its "lose 1 life for each burden counter" ability.

Details and assumptions:
- Phasing means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist: it can't be targeted, its static abilities do nothing, its triggered abilities can't trigger, and it can't attack or block [Teferi's Protection ruling #5]. That's why the phased-out first The One Ring did not stop Avery from having the second The One Ring on the battlefield in the meantime, and why the phased-out copy's upkeep trigger did nothing while phased out.
- Phased-out permanents phase in as Avery's next untap step begins, with counters intact and with any Auras/Equipment that phased out with them [Teferi's Protection ruling #14][Teferi's Protection ruling #15]. Phasing in causes no "enters the battlefield" triggers, so the phased-in The One Ring does not re-trigger its "When The One Ring enters" protection ability [Teferi's Protection ruling #20].
- The second The One Ring, cast after Teferi's Protection, did give Avery protection from everything on entry, but a second instance of protection from the same quality is redundant [702.16m], so it expires along with everything else in the sense that Avery simply has protection from everything until Avery's next turn, then loses it. If Avery's untap step is somehow skipped, the protection and life-total lock still end as the turn begins, but the phased-out permanents wait for the next actual untap step [Teferi's Protection ruling #21].
- Caveat on grounding: the "legend rule" state-based action itself was not included in the rules provided to me (the context includes only the analogous world rule and Role rules, [704.5k] and [704.5y]/[303.7a]), so treat the "keep one, bin the other" step as the standard legend-rule outcome rather than something I can cite here.
- Timing note: I read "the start of the next turn" as Avery's next turn, which is what Teferi's Protection's "until your next turn" duration keys off. If instead the next turn is an opponent's turn, nothing changes yet — Avery's permanents stay phased out and Avery keeps protection from everything and an unchangeable life total through that turn.
- Player count: nothing here depends on the number of opponents; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.113.7a: The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.
gold_text.502.1: First, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that the active player controlled when they phased out phase in. This all happens simultaneously. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. See rule 702.26, “Phasing.”
gold_text.503.1a: The upkeep step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.”) Any abilities that triggered during the untap step and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesn’t matter. (See rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities.”)
gold_text.704.5j: The state-based actions are as follows: If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is called the “legend rule.”

cited_text.702.16m: Protection Multiple instances of protection from the same quality on the same permanent or player are redundant.
cited_text.704.5k: The state-based actions are as follows: If two or more permanents have the supertype world, all except the one that has had the world supertype for the shortest amount of time are put into their owners’ graveyards. In the event of a tie for the shortest amount of time, all are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is called the “world rule.”
cited_text.704.5y: The state-based actions are as follows: If a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner’s graveyard.
cited_text.303.7a: Some Aura enchantments also have the subtype “Role.” If a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner’s graveyard. This is a state-based action. See rule 704.

answer_gold: The One Ring will phase back in during the untap step. Then all triggered abilities will go onto the stack, then before Avery gets priority they will have to sacrifice a The One Ring to state-based actions. When the triggers resolve the trigger affiliated with the sacrificed The One Ring will use last known information to determine how many counters were on it, and how much life Avery should lose.

question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
answer:
Five other permanents — six sacrifices total, one of which is Furnace of Rath.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Both Furnace of Rath and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own ability are replacement effects that modify how that damage would be dealt, so Amaya (the affected permanent's controller) chooses the order they apply [Furnace of Rath ruling #4]. I'm assuming the order the question implies: Furnace of Rath applies first, doubling 3 to 6 damage (the damage still counts as coming from Incinerate, not Furnace of Rath [Furnace of Rath ruling #1]). Then Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement effect converts that into "sacrifice that many permanents" — 6 permanents.

Amaya controls 8 permanents (Dralnu, Lich Lord, Furnace of Rath, and six Snow-Covered Forests), so 6 is payable. Sacrificing means moving a permanent you control from the battlefield straight to its owner's graveyard; it isn't destruction, so regeneration-type effects don't apply [701.21a]. If Furnace of Rath is one of the six, Amaya sacrifices 5 more permanents — and Dralnu, Lich Lord itself is allowed to be one of them [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #4].

If instead Amaya applied Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, there would be no damage left for Furnace of Rath to double, and only 3 permanents would be sacrificed (2 others besides Furnace of Rath). Note also that if the required number ever exceeded Amaya's permanent count, they'd simply sacrifice all permanents they control [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #13]. Nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.616.1: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4).

cited_text.701.21a: Sacrifice To sacrifice a permanent, its controller moves it from the battlefield directly to its owner’s graveyard. A player can’t sacrifice something that isn’t a permanent, or something that’s a permanent they don’t control. Sacrificing a permanent doesn’t destroy it, so regeneration or other effects that replace destruction can’t affect this action.

answer_gold:
Two or five, Amaya's choice.

Both Dralnu, Lich Lord and Furnace of Rath have replacement effects that modify how the game handles damage that is being dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord. As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No — Coral Commando stops attacking. When Arely casts Flash Conscription and gains control of Coral Commando, that change of controller removes Coral Commando from combat: a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. So Coral Commando deals no combat damage in the combat damage step and won't be dealt damage by blockers.

Details and assumptions:
- I'm assuming the timing given: Coral Commando was legally declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step, and Flash Conscription resolved afterward (still during that combat, before combat damage). Under that timing Coral Commando is out of combat for the rest of the phase. If instead Flash Conscription had resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando simply would never have been declared by Aubrey at all (Arely would control it, and Arely could attack with it if Arely were the active player, thanks to the haste it gains).
- Note that although Arely now controls Coral Commando, nothing puts it back into combat. Rule 508.4 only makes a creature attacking if an effect says so or it's put onto the battlefield attacking; Flash Conscription does neither — it only untaps, gains control, and grants haste. Also, once a creature has been declared as an attacker, effects are what remove it from combat, not a re-declaration [506.4a].
- Aubrey has still "attacked" for the purposes of anything that triggered on the declaration, since Coral Commando was declared as an attacker attacking that opponent [508.6].
- Since this is Two-Headed Giant (shared team turns), the attacking team declares one combined set of attackers and announces what each attacker is attacking [805.10b]; that doesn't change the outcome here — the control change still removes Coral Commando from combat. The same answer applies in a plain two-player game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.506.4: A permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield, if its controller changes, if it phases out, if an effect specifically removes it from combat, if it’s a planeswalker that’s being attacked and stops being a planeswalker, if it’s a battle that’s being attacked and stops being a battle, or if it’s an attacking or blocking creature that regenerates (see rule 701.19), stops being a creature, or becomes a battle. A creature that’s removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature. A planeswalker or battle that’s removed from combat stops being attacked.
gold_text.810.5: With the exception of life total and poison counters, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared in the Two-Headed Giant variant. Teammates may review each other’s hands and discuss strategies at any time. Teammates can’t manipulate each other’s cards or permanents.

cited_text.506.4a: A permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield, if its controller changes, if it phases out, if an effect specifically removes it from combat, if it’s a planeswalker that’s being attacked and stops being a planeswalker, if it’s a battle that’s being attacked and stops being a battle, or if it’s an attacking or blocking creature that regenerates (see rule 701.19), stops being a creature, or becomes a battle. A creature that’s removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature. A planeswalker or battle that’s removed from combat stops being attacked. Once a creature has been declared as an attacking or blocking creature, spells or abilities that would have kept that creature from attacking or blocking don’t remove the creature from combat.
cited_text.508.4: If a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects it’s attacking as it enters the battlefield (unless the effect that put it onto the battlefield specifies what it’s attacking). Similarly, if an effect states that a creature is attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects it’s attacking (unless the effect has already specified). Such creatures are “attacking” but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, they never “attacked.” They remain attacking creatures until they’re removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.
cited_text.508.6: A player is “attacking [a player]” if the first player controls a creature that is attacking the second player. A player has “attacked [a player]” if the first player declared one or more creatures as attackers attacking the second player.
cited_text.805.10b: The shared team turns option uses different combat rules than other multiplayer options. As the declare attackers step begins, the active team declares attackers. For each attacking creature, the attacking team announces which defending player, planeswalker, or battle that creature is attacking. The active team has one combined attack, and that set of attacking creatures must be legal as a whole. See rule 508.1.

answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed.

Why: Aubrey's Casualties of War has two chosen modes, "Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature," and both instances of "target" point at the same permanent, Razorfield Thresher. That means it does target only a single permanent, so it's a legal target for Radiate.

Radiate then copies the spell "for each other permanent or player the spell could target," and each copy must target a different one of those permanents/players. Because Casualties of War as cast needs one object to be legal for *both* the artifact target and the creature target, the only permanents it "could target" are artifact creatures. Among Nicolas's permanents, Lake of the Dead is a land (not an artifact, not a creature) and Veinfire Borderpost is an artifact but not a creature, so neither could be a legal target for both instances of "target." Aubrey's Omniscience is an enchantment, also not targetable by the chosen modes. So there is no "other permanent or player the spell could target," and Radiate creates zero copies; Radiate itself does nothing further.

Casualties of War then resolves and destroys Razorfield Thresher (the same permanent for both modes; a permanent can only be destroyed once). Any abilities that trigger on it being destroyed or leaving the battlefield are put on the stack only after Casualties of War finishes resolving [Casualties of War ruling #1], and leaves-the-battlefield triggers "look back in time" at the game state just before it left [603.10a].

One note on how a copy would fare if such a permanent existed: a copy pointed at something that isn't legal for either target instance simply wouldn't resolve; if it were legal for one instance but not the other, it would still resolve and apply only the part it's legal for [608.2b].

Multiplayer: this answer covers Nicolas's and Aubrey's permanents. At a larger table, Radiate would make one copy for each *other* artifact creature on the battlefield that anyone controls (each copy targeting a different one with both modes), and each of those would be destroyed too. Note that Omniscience only affects paying the mana cost; it doesn't change targeting at all.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
gold_text.707.10d: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times Alonso re-applies the copy effect.

Why: Spark Double's text is "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature..." That "except" clause is an additional effect, not a modification of copiable characteristics. Rule 707.9e says that if another copy effect is applied to the object after applying the copy effect carrying such an exception, the exception's effect doesn't happen.

So when Clone copies Spark Double the first time, Clone becomes a copy of Spark Double (Spark Double ruling #7 / Clone ruling #5 confirm chained copying works) and gains Spark Double's copy replacement effect. When Alonso uses that inherited effect to copy Spark Double again, that later copy effect wipes out the earlier exception — no counter from the first application. The same happens for the second and third applications. Only the fourth and final application of the copy effect has no subsequent copy effect applied after it, so only its exception happens: one additional +1/+1 counter (Spark Double ruling #3, which says a Spark Double copying a creature enters with a +1/+1 counter plus any counters from abilities it copied).

So the count doesn't scale with the number of iterations: 1 counter, plus any counters granted by "enters with" abilities of the thing finally copied (here Spark Double has none of its own, such as amplify per 702.38a). Clone also isn't legendary, and that exception *is* copiable (Spark Double ruling #6).

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's purely about how Clone enters, and Spark Double's own restriction is that the copied permanent must be one Alonso controls, so opponents' permanents aren't eligible in any case.

question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life from this pair of permanents — 2 life for Drake Umbra only, and nothing for Nyx Herald, which isn't destroyed.

Why: Fracturing Gust tries to destroy all artifacts and enchantments, which includes both Drake Umbra (an enchantment Aura) and Nyx Herald (an enchantment creature). Drake Umbra's umbra armor is a replacement effect: if the enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy Drake Umbra. Because Fracturing Gust would destroy Nyx Herald and Drake Umbra at the same time, umbra armor saves Nyx Herald, and Fracturing Gust ends up destroying Drake Umbra in two different ways simultaneously — the result is the same as destroying it once [Drake Umbra ruling #4]. Umbra armor's effect is mandatory [Drake Umbra ruling #1].

Since Nyx Herald remains on the battlefield, Ainsley gains no life for it — Fracturing Gust only gives 2 life per permanent actually destroyed by it [Fracturing Gust ruling #0]. Drake Umbra counts once, not twice, so that's 2 life.

Of course, if any other artifacts or enchantments are on the battlefield, add 2 more life for each one Fracturing Gust actually destroys.

Multiplayer note: this outcome doesn't depend on player count; Fracturing Gust hits every player's artifacts and enchantments, so at a bigger table the total is 2 life per permanent destroyed anywhere. In a Two-Headed Giant game, the life gain happens to Ainsley individually but is applied to their team's shared life total [810.9].

question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Rescuer Sphinx's own text is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters: "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Avery chooses Corpsejack Menace as that permanent, and it goes to the owner's hand as part of applying that effect — this all happens while Rescuer Sphinx is entering, and no player may take actions between the choice and Rescuer Sphinx being on the battlefield with its counter [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2]. An effect modifying how a permanent enters the battlefield can indeed cause other objects to change zones [614.13b].

Corpsejack Menace's doubling ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") is a static replacement effect that functions only while Corpsejack Menace is on the battlefield. Because Avery has already returned Corpsejack Menace to hand as part of Rescuer Sphinx entering, it is not on the battlefield to double the counter, so Rescuer Sphinx ends up with a single +1/+1 counter and is a 4/3 flyer.

For contrast: if Avery had returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two +1/+1 counters, since a creature that would enter with +1/+1 counters enters with twice that many [Corpsejack Menace ruling #0] (and four times with two Corpsejack Menaces [Corpsejack Menace ruling #1]).

Note also that Avery couldn't have chosen a permanent entering simultaneously with Rescuer Sphinx — only permanents already on the battlefield are legal choices [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
answer:
Zero copies — assuming Mind's Desire was the first spell cast this turn. Storm counts only spells that were cast *before* the spell with storm this turn ([702.40a]), and Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast afterward (in response), so it is not counted at all.

Details:
- Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" ([702.40a]). The trigger goes on the stack above Mind's Desire; Neil casting Lim-Dûl's Vault in response doesn't change the pool of earlier spells.
- Any spells cast earlier in the turn by *any* player would count, including spells cast from zones other than hand and spells that were countered ([Mind's Desire ruling #3]). So if, say, two spells had already been cast before Arabella's Mind's Desire this turn, the storm trigger would make 2 copies. With none, it makes 0 and the trigger simply resolves doing nothing.
- The copies are put directly onto the stack and aren't cast, so they never count toward a later storm spell's tally ([Mind's Desire ruling #4], [707.10b]). Each copy can be countered individually, and countering the original Mind's Desire doesn't remove the copies ([Mind's Desire ruling #5]); countering the storm trigger itself does prevent all copies ([Mind's Desire ruling #2]).
- Timing note: I'm reading the sequence as Mind's Desire cast first, then Lim-Dûl's Vault cast in response. If instead Neil had cast Lim-Dûl's Vault first and Arabella then cast Mind's Desire, Lim-Dûl's Vault would be an earlier spell and storm would create 1 copy (plus one for any other earlier spell).
- Player count doesn't matter here: storm counts spells cast by all players, so the same reasoning applies in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — just add any spells other opponents cast earlier in the turn.

question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
answer:
Short answer: two cards — the original Bitter Ordeal exiles one card, and the single gravestorm copy exiles a second, assuming Aubrey's Westvale Abbey actually reaches the graveyard before the gravestorm trigger resolves and Natasha's library has at least two cards.

How that adds up:

- Gravestorm on Bitter Ordeal reads "When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent put into a graveyard this turn." Aubrey's first opportunity to act is with that triggered ability still on the stack, so a sacrifice made then happens before the count is taken, giving one permanent (Westvale Abbey) in a graveyard this turn, hence one copy.
- Each of the two Bitter Ordeal objects instructs Aubrey to search Natasha's library for a card and exile it. Searching a hidden zone for a quantity of cards means finding that many cards, or as many as possible if the zone doesn't hold enough [701.23d], and an effect that can't be fully performed does as much as possible [609.3]. So if Natasha's library is down to one card, only one card gets exiled overall; an empty library means none.
- Important caveat about the sacrifice: Westvale Abbey's own ability "{5}, {T}, Sacrifice five creatures: Transform this land, then untap it" sacrifices five *creatures*, not the land itself, and transforming does not put Westvale Abbey into a graveyard. For Westvale Abbey to count for gravestorm, Aubrey needs some outside effect that sacrifices the land. If instead Aubrey activates that ability and sacrifices five creatures, five permanents were put into a graveyard this turn, giving five copies plus the original — six cards exiled from Natasha's library (again, as many as possible if her library is smaller).
- Timing alternative: if the sacrifice somehow happened only after the gravestorm trigger had already resolved, it wouldn't be counted at all and Bitter Ordeal would exile just one card.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table, since Bitter Ordeal targets a single player (Natasha) and gravestorm counts permanents put into any graveyard this turn.

Note on grounding: the provided context has no numbered rule for gravestorm itself, so the copy-count timing above is my stated assumption rather than a cited rule; the search/exile portion is rules-grounded.

question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond. Even with zero targets chosen, Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability goes on the stack and can be responded to.

Why: Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability reads "Any number of target players each lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice. You add {B}{B} and draw a card." "Any number of target players" permits choosing zero targets; a spell or ability like this is still said to require targets, but is only actually "targeted" if one or more targets were chosen [115.6]. So Ainsley may legally activate it with no targets and will still add {B}{B} and draw a card [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0].

Crucially, because the ability *could* have targets, it is not a mana ability, so it does not resolve immediately outside the stack the way an activated mana ability would [605.3b]. It uses the stack and can be responded to even when no targets were chosen [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1]. That means after Ainsley activates it, Ainsley retains priority and then players in turn order get priority, and Nickolas may cast instants or activate abilities in response — including removal on Priest of Forgotten Gods, though that won't stop the already-activated ability from resolving.

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; with more than two players, every opponent gets a chance to respond in turn order, not just Nickolas.

One note on targeting: if Ainsley had chosen targets, players who can't sacrifice a creature are still legal targets and still lose 2 life [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #2].

question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
answer:
No. Analia can't cast Grid Monitor.

Why: because the top card of Analia's graveyard is Grid Monitor, a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter has the full text of Grid Monitor (plus "{2}: Discard a card") [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1, Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]. That text includes "You can't cast creature spells," and Volrath's Shapeshifter is on the battlefield, so that static restriction applies to Analia.

Grid Monitor is an Artifact Creature card, and "creature spell" means any spell with the card type Creature, even if it also has another type such as Artifact [Grid Monitor ruling #1]. So a Grid Monitor spell is a creature spell no matter what.

Muldrotha, the Gravetide would otherwise give permission to cast it from the graveyard as either Analia's artifact-spell or creature-spell play for the turn [Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #0, Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #7], but choosing to "count it as" the artifact permission doesn't change the spell's types — it is still a creature spell. A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it and no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]; Volrath's Shapeshifter (as Grid Monitor) prohibits it, so the prohibition wins over Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission.

Side note on timing: this holds as long as Grid Monitor is the top card of the graveyard at the moment Analia would begin casting. If Analia first changed the top graveyard card (e.g., by discarding with the "{2}: Discard a card" ability so a noncreature card is on top), Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 with no restriction [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0] — but then Grid Monitor is no longer the top card, so Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission isn't limited to the top card anyway and Analia could cast Grid Monitor from anywhere in the graveyard, since Muldrotha, the Gravetide doesn't require it to be on top.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Analia's own permanents are involved.

question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
answer:
No. Antoine cannot cast that Eternal Scourge (or any other card named Eternal Scourge) while it remains exiled by Nico's Ixalan's Binding.

Why: Eternal Scourge says "You may cast this card from exile," which is a permission, and you still must follow normal timing and pay its {3} cost [Eternal Scourge ruling #2]. But Ixalan's Binding says "Your opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card." A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it AND no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]. Since Antoine is an opponent of Nico (Ixalan's Binding's controller), the prohibition applies and overrides the permission granted by Eternal Scourge's own text.

Notes:
- This holds in both two-player and multiplayer games: the lock applies to each opponent of Ixalan's Binding's controller. Nico (and, in multiplayer, Nico's teammates/other non-opponents) would not be stopped by the Binding's restriction, though Eternal Scourge's "you may cast this card from exile" only grants permission to its owner/the exiled card's controller-permission holder, so in practice nobody else gets to cast it either.
- If Ixalan's Binding leaves the battlefield, the exiled Eternal Scourge returns to the battlefield immediately [Ixalan's Binding ruling #4], so it doesn't linger in exile for Antoine to cast.
- The name-matching is based on the card's name as it exists in exile [Ixalan's Binding ruling #2], so any other Eternal Scourge Antoine draws is also uncastable while the Binding is out.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The resulting permanent is a single mutated creature that looks like the face-down manifested card: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no creature types, no mana cost, and mana value 0 — but it has the abilities of both components, i.e. Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token."

Why: when the mutating Trumpeting Gnarr spell resolves with a legal target, it doesn't enter the battlefield; it merges with the manifested creature to form one object represented by both cards, and Avery chooses the order [702.140c, 608.3d, 730.2a]. Because Avery puts the manifested (face-down) card on top, all characteristics other than abilities are derived from that topmost component [702.140e, 730.2a], and a face-down manifested permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities, mana value 0 [Soul Summons ruling #8]. Abilities are the exception: a mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it [702.140e], so the Trumpeting Gnarr card underneath still contributes its two abilities even though it isn't the top card.

That mutate trigger does go off: an ability that triggers whenever a creature mutates triggers when a spell merges with a creature as a result of a resolving mutating creature spell, so Avery creates one 3/3 green Beast token [702.140d].

Also note Avery can still turn the manifested top card face up as a special action any time they have priority, by revealing it's a creature card and paying its mana cost [Soul Summons ruling #6, Soul Summons ruling #2]; if they do, the topmost component's face-up characteristics (name, colors, types, power/toughness) become the mutated permanent's characteristics, and it keeps Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities on top of its own. If the manifested card isn't a creature card, it can't be turned face up [Soul Summons ruling #1].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; mutate targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as the spell, so it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table [702.140a].

question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
answer:
No — Ariel gains no life. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so while Golgari Brownscale sits in Ariel's graveyard it has no abilities at all, including its "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life" triggered ability.

That ability is one that must trigger while the card is still in the graveyard (the trigger event is leaving the graveyard for the hand), so the game looks at Golgari Brownscale in the graveyard to see whether it has the ability — and thanks to Yixlid Jailer, it doesn't. This matches the principle in [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4]: abilities that trigger on the object moving out of / into the graveyard from somewhere other than the battlefield are looked for in the graveyard, and Yixlid Jailer stops them from triggering at all. Contrast [Yixlid Jailer ruling #6]: only abilities that trigger from the battlefield escape Yixlid Jailer, which isn't the case here.

Disturbing Plot returning Golgari Brownscale is just an ordinary return-to-hand, so nothing else grants the ability, and no life gain event occurs at all — not even 0 life (see [119.3], [119.9]). It doesn't matter that Nayeli, not Ariel, controls Yixlid Jailer; its static effect applies to cards in all graveyards.

If Ariel later casts Golgari Brownscale or it otherwise reaches the battlefield, it has its abilities again there — but that gives no retroactive life gain. Note also that if Disturbing Plot is conspired and copied, targeting Golgari Brownscale again does nothing since it's already in hand.

This answer is the same at any table size; nothing here depends on the number of players.

question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
Yes. Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap normally during Noe's untap step. Exert means "you choose to have it not untap during your next untap step" — the untap step of the player who exerted it, i.e. Aryana [701.43a]. Because Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's third ability only gains control of Ahn-Crop Crasher until end of turn, control reverts to Noe when Aryana's turn ends, and Ahn-Crop Crasher is never around under Aryana's control for Aryana's own next untap step. Exert's effect places no restriction on Noe's untap step, so during Noe's untap step Noe (the active player) untaps Ahn-Crop Crasher along with their other permanents as a turn-based action [502.3], [703.4c]. This is exactly the case covered by the card ruling: if you gain control of another player's creature until end of turn and exert it, it untaps during that player's untap step [Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #4].

Note that no player gets priority during the untap step, so nothing can be done at that moment to interfere [502.4]. If Aryana somehow still controlled Ahn-Crop Crasher when Aryana's next untap step arrived, the exert effect would apply then and keep it tapped; and if it were already untapped at that time, the effect would simply expire doing nothing [Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #2]. The answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — what matters is that Ahn-Crop Crasher is back under Noe's control, and Noe's own untap step untaps it.

Then they untap them all simultaneously. See rule 502.3.

answer_gold: Yes. A player exerting a permanent only causes it to not untap during that player's next untap step, not any untap step that would untap it.

question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?
answer:
As Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability resolves, "the exiled card" refers to both cards exiled by the Hideaway 4 trigger and its copy, so Andres may play either one, both, or neither of them without paying their mana costs — provided he controls four or more legendary creatures at that time.

Why: Hideaway 4 on Clive's Hideaway is a triggered ability that exiles a card face down [702.75a], and it is linked to Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability that refers to "the exiled card" [607.2a]. When Strionic Resonator copies that triggered ability, the copy is also linked to the same second ability, so "the exiled card" means every card exiled by the original trigger and the copy [Strionic Resonator ruling #1]. Where such a linked ability asks about "the exiled card" and gets multiple answers, it applies to all of them [Strionic Resonator ruling #3].

Practical notes: the permission is "you may play," so playing is optional and each card is played separately as the ability resolves; playing a land this way still uses no mana but does use his land play for the turn, and a nonland card is cast without paying its mana cost. The four-or-more-legendary-creatures condition is checked as Andres actually plays a card, so if he loses legendary creatures midway he can't continue. Also, Strionic Resonator's copy doesn't grant anything an ability — it just puts a second instance of the Hideaway trigger on the stack [Strionic Resonator ruling #0], and the copy's own look-at-top-four/exile choices were made separately when the copy resolved [Strionic Resonator ruling #7].

This interaction works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
answer:
No — Aminah doesn't lose the game, provided the {1} ability of Words of Wind is active when the draw would happen.

Why: Words of Wind's ability says "The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand instead." That's a replacement effect for a card draw. An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because the affected player's library is empty [121.6a]. So when Aminah's draw step arrives, the draw is replaced by the returning of permanents; Aminah never actually attempts to draw from the empty library, so the state-based action that makes a player who attempted to draw from an empty library lose the game never applies [121.4], [704.5b].

Timing assumption: activating Words of Wind during the upkeep step happens before Aminah's draw step, so the shield is in place for the turn's normal draw. If instead Aminah had already been required to draw from the empty library earlier (before any Words of Wind replacement was available), that attempted draw already set up the loss and Aminah would lose the next time a player would receive priority [121.4], [704.5b] — activating Words of Wind afterward wouldn't undo it. Also note the replacement only covers "the next time" one draw; a second unreplaced draw from the empty library that turn would still cause the loss. If Aminah activated Words of Wind multiple times, they choose which instance to apply and use up on each draw [Words of Wind ruling #0].

Multiplayer: the outcome for Aminah is the same with two players or more. The difference is only in scope of the replacement — "each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand," so at a larger table every opponent also bounces one of their permanents.

question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
answer:
Runeclaw Bear is dealt 8 damage — the full amount Allan divided when activating Living Inferno's ability. Chemister's Trick's -2/-0 does not reduce it.

Because Living Inferno's ability divides damage among targets, the amount of damage is locked in as the ability is activated, based on Living Inferno's power at that time (8). Later changes to Living Inferno's power — including Chemister's Trick making it a 6/5 until end of turn — don't change how much damage the ability deals [Living Inferno ruling #0][Living Inferno ruling #1]. Runeclaw Bear (2/2) dies from the 8 damage.

By contrast, the damage the targeted creatures deal back to Living Inferno is not locked in; it's determined on resolution [Living Inferno ruling #1]. So Runeclaw Bear deals 2 damage (its power at resolution, per the general rule that damage equals power) to Living Inferno, which is a 6/5 at that point, so it survives with 2 damage marked.

Note also that Chemister's Trick makes Living Inferno "attack this turn if able," but Living Inferno will be tapped from paying {T}, and a tapped creature doesn't attack [Chemister's Trick ruling #0].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
answer:
Yes. Adrian may reveal Chancellor of the Annex from their opening hand for its reveal ability and then exile that same Chancellor of the Annex as the cost of putting Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield.

Why this works:

- Revealing a card doesn't move it out of your hand — "revealing a card doesn't cause it to leave the zone it's in" [701.20b]. So after revealing Chancellor of the Annex, it is still a card in Adrian's opening hand and is therefore still a legal choice for Gemstone Caverns' "exile a card from your hand."
- Both cards are opening-hand-action cards. Once mulligans are done, the starting player takes all such actions first, in any order, then each other player in turn order [103.6], [103.6a], [103.6b], [Gemstone Caverns ruling #0], [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #2]. Adrian is going second, so Adrian acts after the starting player, and Adrian may take these two actions in either order.
- Gemstone Caverns' own text requires that Adrian not be the starting player, which is satisfied here; Adrian begins the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield with a luck counter on it (so it can tap for one mana of any color).
- Chancellor of the Annex's revealed ability creates the game-long delayed trigger: when each opponent casts their first spell of the game, counter it unless that player pays {1} (that's one generic mana, payable with any color or colorless). Note {1}, not {C}. The reveal itself is what sets this up; exiling the card afterward as Gemstone Caverns' cost doesn't undo the reveal. Practical order tip: reveal Chancellor of the Annex first (or at least clearly announce the reveal), since a card in exile is no longer being revealed from your opening hand.
- Sequencing caveat: the rules say a card revealed this way "remains revealed until the first turn begins" [103.6b]. If your table insists the physical card stay revealed in hand until the first turn, resolve it by keeping Chancellor of the Annex visible as you exile it — either way the ability applies once the reveal was legally made. If instead Adrian exiles Chancellor of the Annex to Gemstone Caverns *without* first revealing it, no ability is set up at all.

Two players vs. more: with only one opponent, the trigger applies once, to that opponent's first spell. In a multiplayer game, Chancellor of the Annex triggers for each opponent's first spell of the game [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #1], and the opening-hand actions still proceed starting player first, then each other player in turn order [103.6b]. Gemstone Caverns works the same for any non-starting player.

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Both cards end up in exile, and the merged permanent stops existing as one object.

Details:

1. Merging: when Aspen cast Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt for its mutate cost targeting Cosima, God of the Voyage and put it underneath, the two cards became a single mutated permanent that has all abilities of both cards, with its other characteristics (name, types, power/toughness) taken from the top card, Cosima, God of the Voyage [702.140c] [702.140e]. So the permanent is named Cosima, God of the Voyage, is a 2/4 God, and has double strike, the Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt mutate trigger, and Cosima, God of the Voyage's upkeep ability.

2. The upkeep ability triggers because that permanent is on the battlefield and is named Cosima, God of the Voyage; Aspen may exile it only if it's still on the battlefield as the ability resolves [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #13].

3. When Aspen exiles it, the merged permanent leaves the battlefield as one permanent, but the individual component cards — the Cosima, God of the Voyage card and the Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt card — are each put into exile as separate objects, and Aspen (the player exiling it) determines their relative timestamp order at that time [730.3b]. An effect that can find the new object the merged permanent became finds all of those objects, and takes the same action on each [730.3c]. They are no longer merged, so the Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt card is just a separate exiled card; it does not re-merge if anything returns to the battlefield.

4. Because the granted ability applies to what was exiled, it applies to those exiled objects, and each returns as its own card (front face up for the modal double-faced Cosima, God of the Voyage) if Aspen later chooses to return rather than add a voyage counter [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #9] [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #5]. The granted ability's intervening-if checks that Cosima, God of the Voyage is still exiled when it tries to resolve; if it has left exile, the ability does nothing [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #11].

5. No mutate trigger occurs from any of this — the Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt trigger only fires when a mutating creature spell merges with a creature [702.140d].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the mutate had fully resolved before the upkeep trigger, as stated. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt both get exiled and gain the corresponding triggered ability.

question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
answer:
No. Whiskervale Forerunner's valiant ability does not trigger a second time, for two independent reasons.

First, the copy of Growth Cycle created by Cooperate doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner at all — Aubrey changed the copy's target to another creature, and Cooperate/copy rules let you choose new targets for the copy ([707.10e], [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #18]). A valiant ability only triggers when that creature itself becomes the target.

Second, even if Aubrey had left the copy pointed at Whiskervale Forerunner, valiant reads "becomes the target of a spell or ability you control for the first time each turn." The original Growth Cycle already used up that once-per-turn trigger, so a copy targeting it again this turn would do nothing. (A copy targeting a valiant creature does trigger valiant, but only if the creature hasn't yet been targeted by a spell or ability you control that turn — [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #1].)

Timing note: I'm assuming the order given — Growth Cycle cast (valiant triggers and, per [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #2], resolves before Growth Cycle), then Cooperate cast and resolved, putting the copy on the stack. The copy resolves before the original Growth Cycle ([Refuse // Cooperate ruling #14]). If instead the copy had been made and retargeted onto a *different* valiant creature Aubrey controls that hadn't been targeted yet this turn, that other creature's valiant would trigger.

Side note on size: the copy's bonus is locked in as it begins to resolve, and Growth Cycle itself is still on the stack (not in the graveyard) at that time, so the copy gives just +3/+3 plus +2/+2 for each *other* card named Growth Cycle already in Aubrey's graveyard ([Growth Cycle ruling #0], [Growth Cycle ruling #1]).

This answer is the same regardless of how many players are at the table; nothing here depends on player count.

question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
answer:
Short answer: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its three +1/+1 counters all the way onto the battlefield, so it's manifested as a face-down 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it (a 5/5). That makes it obvious to everyone, including Nico, which face-down permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave — the other one, the manifested Pillarfield Ox, is a plain 2/2 with no counters.

Why: normally counters simply cease to exist when an object changes zones ([122.2]). Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text overrides that general rule: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule. Ghastly Conscription moves it graveyard → exile, then exile → battlefield; neither is a hand or library, and the ability functions as long as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has that ability in the zone it's moving from ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]) — it does in the graveyard and in exile. It also retains all kinds of counters, not just +1/+1 ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5]). Note the counters aren't "put on" it, so counter-doubling/counter-hating effects don't interact with them ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #0]).

The face-down permanent itself is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]), and +1/+1 counters still apply to its power/toughness, hence 5/5. The face-down permanent no longer has Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's counter-retention ability, so if it later leaves the battlefield while still face down, those counters will cease to exist ([122.2]).

On hidden information: the shuffling of the face-down pile is meant to disguise which manifested creature is which ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #3]), but the counters give it away here. Arjun cast the spell and manifests the cards, so Arjun controls both face-down permanents and may look at them ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #13]); Nico doesn't get to look at them, but Nico can deduce from the counters that the 5/5 is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and the counter-less 2/2 is Pillarfield Ox. Either can be turned face up by its controller paying its mana cost as a special action ({B}{G} for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, {3}{W} for Pillarfield Ox) ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #2]).

This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer table; Ghastly Conscription targets a single player (Nico) either way. One extra multiplayer note: if Arjun leaves the game, the manifested cards Nico owns are exiled ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #6]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

However, if a player is instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or once a player is allowed to look at a card exiled face down, that player may continue to look at that card until it leaves the exile zone or is part of a pile of cards that are shuffled, even if the instruction allowing the player to do so no longer applies.
