answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nico will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Pillarfield Ox.

question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
answer:
Ascendant Spirit will phase back in as it was before: a 1/1 base Snow Creature — Spirit, now with the +1/+1 counter Slip Out the Back gave it, so it's a 2/2 Spirit — not a Spirit Warrior with base 2/3.

Why: Slip Out the Back was cast after the ability was activated, so Slip Out the Back is on top of the stack and resolves first. It puts a +1/+1 counter on Ascendant Spirit and phases it out. "Phased out" is a status meaning the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist — it can't be targeted, its abilities can't trigger, and effects can't apply to it [110.5c], [Slip Out the Back ruling #1]. When Ascendant Spirit's first ability ({S}{S}: becomes a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3) then tries to resolve, its source is phased out and treated as nonexistent, so the type-and-base-P/T change does nothing. That ability isn't a duration-based effect that waits around; nothing reapplies it later [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8].

It phases in during Avery's next untap step, immediately before Avery untaps their permanents, and its status changes back to "phased in" [702.26a], [502.1], [702.26c], [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Counters are kept through phasing, so the +1/+1 counter is still there [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Any Auras or Equipment attached to Ascendant Spirit phased out with it and phase back in still attached [702.26g], [Slip Out the Back ruling #5]. It can attack and use {T} costs that turn [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. If Ascendant Spirit was attacking or blocking, phasing out removed it from combat [Slip Out the Back ruling #0].

Assumed timing: the activated ability was still on the stack when Slip Out the Back resolved. If instead the {S}{S} ability had resolved first and then Slip Out the Back phased it out, Ascendant Spirit would phase back in as a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3 plus the +1/+1 counter (a 3/4), since that effect has no duration.

This works identically with two players or more than two — phasing in is keyed to the controller's own untap step, not to any opponent count.

There are four status categories, each of which has two possible values: tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, face up/face down, and phased in/phased out. Each permanent always has one of these values for each of these categories. Through use of Jushi Apprentice’s ability, this creature flips, making it a copy of Tomoya the Revealer with the Dimir Doppelganger ability. If this permanent then becomes a copy of Runeclaw Bear, it will retain its flipped status even though that has no relevance to Runeclaw Bear. During each player’s untap step, before the active player untaps permanents, all phased-in permanents with phasing that player controls “phase out.” Simultaneously, all phased-out permanents that had phased out under that player’s control “phase in.”

This alternate way of phasing out is known as phasing out “indirectly.” An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification that phased out indirectly won’t phase in by itself, but instead phases in along with the permanent it’s attached to.

answer_gold: It will be a 2/2 and not a Warrior. When Ascendant Spirit's ability resolves it's phased out and won't be affected.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives first, and then the devour replacement effects of the tokens.

Why: creating a token is an event that *contains* the event of that token entering the battlefield. Rule 616.1g says that when one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer effect must be chosen first — the second can't be chosen until the first has been applied. That's exactly the Doubling Season/Voice of All example in 616.1g, and Parallel Lives has the same doubling text. So Parallel Lives doubles the number of tokens first (unkicked Rite of Replication: 1 token becomes 2; kicked: 5 becomes 10), and only then does each token's devour 1 replacement effect (from copying Caldera Hellion) get applied.

Once Parallel Lives has been applied, each token does get its own devour choice, and the choices are made before the tokens enter (614.12a; Caldera Hellion ruling #3, Rite of Replication ruling #11). But a single creature can only be sacrificed for one of them: 614.13b and Caldera Hellion ruling #3 state the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how permanents enter. So sacrificing 1 creature gives exactly one token a single +1/+1 counter, not all of them. Also, the tokens can't devour each other or the original Caldera Hellion's fellow enterers — you may only sacrifice creatures already on the battlefield (614.13a, Caldera Hellion ruling #1), though the original Caldera Hellion on the battlefield is a legal sacrifice for one token.

Note each token also has Caldera Hellion's triggered ability dealing 3 damage to each creature, so a token with only one +1/+1 counter (4/4) survives one instance but the tokens will finish each other off as those triggers resolve (Caldera Hellion ruling #4).

This interaction doesn't depend on the number of players; it's all within Aspen's own choices. If other players controlled replacement effects applying at the same time, those choices would be made in APNAP order (616.1).

answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all.

Exotic Orchard reads "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land an opponent (Nikolas) controls is Crumbling Vestige, whose mana-producing activated ability is "{T}: Add {C}" — colorless mana. {C} is colorless mana specifically; it is not a color. The five colors of mana are white, blue, black, red, and green, and Exotic Orchard can never be tapped for colorless mana even if an opponent's land could produce colorless mana [Exotic Orchard ruling #3]. So there is no color of mana Exotic Orchard can name here.

When a mana ability would produce mana of an undefined type, it produces no mana instead [106.5], and 106.7 confirms that if nothing satisfies the "could produce" check, there's no type of mana it could produce — the same way Exotic Orchard yields nothing when an opponent controls no lands [106.7]. Aubrey still taps Exotic Orchard (paying {T}) and simply gets nothing.

Note on Crumbling Vestige's other ability: "When this land enters, add one mana of any color" is a triggered ability that only functions as Crumbling Vestige enters the battlefield, so at the time Aubrey activates Exotic Orchard it isn't an ability that would produce colored mana if it resolved then. Even if you tried to count it, Exotic Orchard's check is limited to what it can name as a color of mana at that moment, and the assumption here is that Crumbling Vestige is already on the battlefield, not entering. If instead the two things happened simultaneously — i.e., you're asking about the moment Crumbling Vestige's enters-the-battlefield trigger is on the stack — that trigger still hasn't been chosen/resolved, so it does not give Exotic Orchard a color to name.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players: Exotic Orchard looks at lands any opponent controls, so at a multiplayer table you would also check every other opponent's lands, and any of them that could produce a color of mana would let Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produce that color [Exotic Orchard ruling #4].

question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Azariah can see which opponent Beckham secretly chose for Stalking Leonin.

While controlling Beckham, Azariah sees all information about objects in the game that Beckham can see — that includes Beckham's hand, the faces of face-down creatures Beckham controls, and hidden game information like the note recording the secret choice made when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield [723.4]. Worst Fears itself says "You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them," and its rulings confirm you see all cards in the game that player can see [Worst Fears ruling #11]. Since the secret choice for Stalking Leonin is recorded and kept with the card (for example, by writing the player's name on a piece of paper kept with Stalking Leonin) [Stalking Leonin ruling #2], that recorded choice is in-game information about a permanent Beckham controls, not information about cards outside the game (which would stay hidden from Azariah) [723.4].

Two related points: Azariah doesn't gain control of Stalking Leonin itself — only control of Beckham changes, and all permanents stay under their normal controllers [723.3][Worst Fears ruling #4]. But because Azariah makes all choices and decisions Beckham is allowed to make during that turn, Azariah decides whether to activate Stalking Leonin's reveal ability, paying with Beckham's resources only [723.5b][Worst Fears ruling #1][Worst Fears ruling #8]. If Azariah does reveal, the ability only exiles an attacking creature that's controlled by the previously chosen player and is attacking Beckham (Beckham remains the active player and the player being attacked matters, not Azariah) [723.3][Worst Fears ruling #7]; a creature attacking a planeswalker isn't attacking Beckham and can't be targeted [Stalking Leonin ruling #4].

This is inherently a multiplayer answer: with three players there really is a chosen opponent other than Azariah possible, and Azariah learning the secret choice is a genuine information gain. In a two-player game the choice would trivially have to be the only opponent anyway.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.722.4: In every zone, a preparation card has only its normal characteristics.

cited_text.723.4: If information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible to both that player and the controller of the player. If information about cards outside the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible only to that player, not the controller of the player. The controller of a player can see that player’s hand and the face of any face-down creatures they control.
cited_text.723.3: Only control of the player changes. All objects are controlled by their normal controllers. A player who’s being controlled during their turn is still the active player.
cited_text.723.5b: While controlling another player, a player makes all choices and decisions the controlled player is allowed to make or is told to make by the rules or by any objects. This includes choices and decisions about what to play, and choices and decisions called for by spells and abilities. The controller of another player can’t make choices or decisions for that player that aren’t called for by the rules or by any objects. The controller also can’t make any choices or decisions for the player that would be called for by the tournament rules. The player who’s being controlled still decides if they will leave to visit the restroom, trade a card to someone else, agree to an intentional draw, or call a judge about an error or infraction.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
Angela can't declare any meaningful band at all.

Why: none of the four attackers has plain banding. The only banding-type ability in play is "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," granted by Master of the Hunt to its Wolves of the Hunt tokens.

- Master of the Hunt itself has no banding ability, and neither does the Sakashima the Impostor that entered as a copy of Master of the Hunt (copying Master of the Hunt copies its token-making activated ability, not banding).
- The Sakashima the Impostor that entered as a copy of a Wolves of the Hunt token does have "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but Sakashima the Impostor's copy effect explicitly keeps its name as Sakashima the Impostor. That card text overrides the normal copy rule for names.
- Under rule 702.22c, a "bands with other [quality]" band may only contain attacking creatures that themselves have that quality — here, creatures named Wolves of the Hunt. That Sakashima the Impostor is not named Wolves of the Hunt, so it cannot legally be a member of such a band, even though it supplies the ability.

That leaves only the single Wolves of the Hunt token as an eligible band member, and a "band" of one creature accomplishes nothing (no other creature becomes blocked with it, per 702.22h/702.22i). So the answer is: zero bands.

If Angela had a second actual Wolves of the Hunt token on the battlefield and attacked with it, she could band the two tokens together (at least one has the ability), and per 702.22d/802.3b all creatures in that band would have to attack the same player, planeswalker, or battle. Mirror Gallery is relevant only in that it switches off the legend rule so both legendary Sakashima the Impostor permanents can coexist; it has no effect on banding.

This analysis is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; the only multiplayer wrinkle is the 702.22d/802.3b requirement that a band's members can't be split across different defending players or their planeswalkers/battles.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
All four permanents phase out during Avery's untap step, and none phase in during that same untap step (nothing was already phased out). At Avery's next untap step, the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter phase back in, and the two Teferi's Curses phase in along with them.

Details:

- Phasing means a permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out, without changing zones or control (702.26a, 702.26d).
- The Germ token has phasing from the Teferi's Curse enchanting it, and Barbed Bloodletter has phasing from the Teferi's Curse enchanting it. Both the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter are controlled by Avery, so during Avery's untap step, before Avery untaps anything, both phase out directly (502.1, 702.26a, 703.4a).
- The two Teferi's Curses are Nadia's, and they don't have phasing themselves, so they never phase out on their own during Avery's untap step. But an Aura attached to a permanent that phases out phases out at the same time — "indirectly." So the Teferi's Curse on the Germ token phases out indirectly with the Germ token, and the Teferi's Curse on Barbed Bloodletter phases out indirectly with Barbed Bloodletter (702.26g).
- Phasing in: only permanents that phased out under a player's control phase in during that player's untap step. The Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter phased out under Avery's control, so they phase in at Avery's next untap step (702.26a, 703.4a). The Teferi's Curses phased out indirectly, so they can't phase in by themselves (they will not phase in during Nadia's untap step); they phase in along with the permanents they're attached to (702.26g).
- The Germ token doesn't cease to exist while phased out, and counters/stickers on the permanents stay (702.26d).
- Note that when the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter phase out, they'll immediately phase back out again at each of Avery's untap steps as long as the Curses stay attached — the phase-in and phase-out happen simultaneously at the untap step, so in practice they phase in during Avery's untap step and, being phased in with phasing, that same turn-based action is what determines it; the sequencing is: everything phased in and phased out is resolved simultaneously (502.1, 702.26a).

Multiplayer: the same answer applies with two players or more, since phasing keys off each player's own untap step. One extra multiplayer rule: if a permanent phased out under the control of a player who then leaves the game, it phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun (702.26n). If Avery's untap step is skipped, the phasing event simply doesn't happen that turn (702.26m).

question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
answer:
Nobody gains or loses any life. Alessandra doesn't gain 14, and no opponent loses 14.

Why: Day's Undoing has each player shuffle hand and graveyard into their library and draw seven cards, then — because it's Alessandra's own turn — it ends the turn. Sheoldred, the Apocalypse's two triggered abilities ("Whenever you draw a card, you gain 2 life" and "Whenever an opponent draws a card, they lose 2 life") do trigger on those draws (7 triggers for Alessandra, 7 for each opponent), but they are still waiting to be put onto the stack when Day's Undoing finishes resolving and ends the turn. [Day's Undoing ruling #5] says that abilities which trigger while players are shuffling cards into their library or drawing seven cards cease to exist when the turn ends — they are never put onto the stack, so they never resolve and never change any life total. [Day's Undoing ruling #4] also confirms that ending the turn exiles everything on the stack and no player gets priority, and [Day's Undoing ruling #0] notes exiled spells/abilities aren't "countered."

This is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: each opponent draws seven and triggers Sheoldred, the Apocalypse's second ability seven times, but every one of those triggers ceases to exist, so no opponent loses life regardless of how many opponents there are.

Timing note: this assumes Day's Undoing was cast on Alessandra's own turn, as stated. If it resolved during someone else's turn, the turn would not end, all 14 triggers would go on the stack after Day's Undoing finished resolving, and then Alessandra would gain 2 life per card drawn (14 total) and each opponent would lose 2 life per card drawn (14 each), adjusting life totals normally per 119.3.

In a Two-Headed Giant game those individual gains/losses would each be applied to the team's shared life total (810.9), but here there's nothing to apply.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.723.1a: Some cards allow a player to control another player during that player’s next turn. This effect applies to the next turn that the affected player actually takes. The affected player is controlled during the entire turn; the effect doesn’t end until the beginning of the next turn. Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works.

cited_text.119.3: If an effect causes a player to gain life or lose life, that player’s life total is adjusted accordingly.

In a Two-Headed Giant game, a player casts Flame Rift, which reads, “Flame Rift deals 4 damage to each player.” Each team is dealt a total of 8 damage.

question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
answer:
Nothing happens to it — Lazotep Convert stays as it is (a copy of Kessig Naturalist, a 2/2 Human Werewolf with daybound) and does not transform when it becomes night.

Why: daybound is a set of static abilities, one of which reads "As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it," plus "This permanent can't transform except due to its daybound ability" [702.145b]. The corresponding check in [702.145c] only transforms a permanent that is *front face up* with daybound while it's night. Adonis's permanent is the physical card Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert with its **back** face (Lazotep Convert) up — the copy effect changes its copiable characteristics, not which face of the card is up. Since it is not front face up, the daybound transform instruction simply doesn't apply, and no other effect can transform it [702.145b]. It also doesn't have nightbound, so [702.145f] is irrelevant.

Even setting that aside, transforming it would turn it into Invasion of Amonkhet, a battle — the copy effect wouldn't survive the face change in the way you'd want, and the rules generally refuse to transform/convert into an illegal face (compare [701.28d], and the analogous ruling in [712.13a] where a would-be transform into an instant/sorcery face is simply not carried out). The practical point stands: it stays a Kessig Naturalist copy.

Assumption on timing: it doesn't matter whether night arrives during the untap-step day/night check [502.2] or from some other effect mid-turn; the daybound check happens "any time" the condition is met [702.145c] and it fails either way.

Day/night is a designation of the game itself [731.1], so this is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is the shared-team-turns variant for whether it becomes night/day at all [731.2a], [731.2b].

Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
answer:
Yes — provided Thwart the Enemy resolves before Fireblade Charger's death trigger resolves and deals its damage, that damage is prevented and simply never happens.

How it works:
- Fireblade Charger's death trigger goes on the stack when it dies. Nasir can respond to that trigger by casting Thwart the Enemy. Because a prevention effect must already exist when the damage event would occur (rule 615.4), casting Thwart the Enemy while the trigger is still on the stack is in time; if Nasir instead waits until Fireblade Charger's ability has already resolved and dealt the damage, it's too late and nothing is prevented.
- "Prevent" means the damage is not dealt at all (rule 615.1a, glossary "Prevent"). Since all of Fireblade Charger's damage is prevented, it never happens (rule 615.6), and abilities that trigger on damage being dealt won't trigger (rule 603.2g). Fireblade Charger's ability still resolves; its instruction just can't be carried out.
- The source is Fireblade Charger, which is in Adelina's graveyard by then. Its characteristics — including that it was a creature Adelina (Nasir's opponent) controlled, and its power — are taken from its last existence on the battlefield (Fireblade Charger ruling #0). So it matches Thwart the Enemy's description of "creatures your opponents control" (see also rules 609.7b/609.7c on rechecking a source's properties). If Fireblade Charger's last-known power was 0 or less, the ability does nothing anyway.
- If Fireblade Charger's damage were somehow made unpreventable, Thwart the Enemy would still be applied but would prevent nothing (rule 615.12a).

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players — Thwart the Enemy prevents damage from creatures controlled by any of Nasir's opponents, so Adelina's Fireblade Charger is covered regardless of table size, and the damage is prevented no matter which player or permanent the ability targeted.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.113.7a: The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.

cited_text.615.4: Prevention effects must exist before the appropriate damage event occurs—they can’t “go back in time” and change something that’s already happened. Spells or abilities that generate these effects are often cast or activated in response to whatever would produce the event and thus resolve before that event would occur. A player can activate an ability that prevents damage in response to a spell that would deal damage. Once the spell resolves, though, it’s too late to prevent the damage.
cited_text.615.1a: Some continuous effects are prevention effects. Like replacement effects (see rule 614), prevention effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevent the damage that would be dealt. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “prevent” are prevention effects. Prevention effects use “prevent” to indicate what damage will not be dealt.
cited_text.615.6: If damage that would be dealt is prevented, it never happens. A modified event may occur instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
cited_text.603.2g: Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesn’t do anything at this point. An ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs. An event that’s prevented or replaced won’t trigger anything. An ability that triggers on damage being dealt won’t trigger if all the damage is prevented.
cited_text.609.7b: Some effects apply to damage from a source—for example, “The next time a red source of your choice would deal damage to you this turn, prevent that damage.” Some effects from resolved spells and abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties, such as a creature or a source of a particular color. When the source would deal damage, the “shield” rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced. If for any reason the shield prevents no damage or replaces no damage, the shield isn’t used up.
cited_text.609.7c: Some effects apply to damage from a source—for example, “The next time a red source of your choice would deal damage to you this turn, prevent that damage.” Some effects from static abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties. For these effects, the prevention or replacement applies to sources that are permanents with that property and to any sources that aren’t on the battlefield that have that property.
cited_text.615.12a: Some effects state that damage “can’t be prevented.” If unpreventable damage would be dealt, any applicable prevention effects are still applied to it. Those effects won’t prevent any damage, but any additional effects they have will take place. Existing damage prevention shields won’t be reduced by damage that can’t be prevented. A prevention effect is applied to any particular unpreventable damage event just once. It won’t invoke itself repeatedly trying to prevent that damage.
cited_text.Prevent: Prevent. A word used by prevention effects to indicate what damage will not be dealt. See rule 615, “Prevention Effects.”

answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
After Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls both. Analia controls Corrupted Conscience (Lay Claim says "You control enchanted permanent," and it's Analia's Lay Claim), and because Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature," its "you" now refers to its new controller, Analia — so Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard again.

Why: control-changing effects are all applied in layer 2 (rule 613.1b). Lay Claim's effect changes who controls Corrupted Conscience; Corrupted Conscience's effect is controller-dependent, so once Analia is its controller, it hands Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia rather than to Nico. Note that an Aura's controller is separate from the controller of what it enchants, and changing control of one doesn't automatically change control of the other (rules 303.4e, and Lay Claim ruling #0) — here the swap happens only because Corrupted Conscience's own text points at "you."

Also worth noting: an ability that triggers when a player loses control of an object (Nico losing Corrupted Conscience and Bane Alley Blackguard) looks back in time (rule 603.10d), though neither card here has such a trigger. If Analia's Lay Claim later leaves the battlefield, Corrupted Conscience reverts to Nico's control and Bane Alley Blackguard goes back to Nico as well.

This works the same regardless of table size; if a player leaves a multiplayer game, rule 800.4a governs — e.g., if Analia left, her Lay Claim would leave with her and Nico would control Corrupted Conscience and thus Bane Alley Blackguard again.

For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied.
gold_text.613.7: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp.
gold_text.613.7a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment “Equipped creature has flying.” A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with “Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.” The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of Flight’s timestamp because it is later than Colossus Hammer’s timestamp. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object or player.
gold_text.613.8a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect is said to “depend on” another if (a) it’s applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.
gold_text.613.8b: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied. If multiple dependent effects would apply simultaneously in this way, they’re applied in timestamp order relative to each other. If several dependent effects form a dependency loop, then this rule is ignored and the effects in the dependency loop are applied in timestamp order.

For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied.
cited_text.303.4e: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura enchants an object, changing control of the object doesn’t change control of the Aura, and vice versa. Only the Aura’s controller can activate its abilities. answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Autumn controls [Traveling Chocobo] and casts [Phyrexian Ingester]. Autumn exiles [Scarwood Goblins] and then [Tor Giant] with the triggers. What are Phyrexian Ingester's power and toughness?
answer:
Phyrexian Ingester ends up 5/5 — and it only exiles one creature, not two. Traveling Chocobo's last ability only doubles triggers caused by a *land or Bird* you control entering the battlefield; Phyrexian Ingester is a Phyrexian Beast, so its Imprint trigger ("When this creature enters, you may exile target nontoken creature") triggers only once. Autumn exiles just one of the two — say Scarwood Goblins, a 2/2 — and Phyrexian Ingester's second ability gives it +2/+2 over its printed 3/3, so it's 5/5 (Tor Giant stays on the battlefield). If Autumn instead exiled Tor Giant (3/3), Phyrexian Ingester would be 6/6.

Details:
- Traveling Chocobo's text is what governs here: only a land or Bird entering causes an extra trigger, so no second Imprint trigger exists ([Traveling Chocobo ruling #12] confirms it applies to a permanent's own "enters" triggers only when that permanent is a land or Bird you control).
- The bonus uses the exiled card's power/toughness as they are in the exile zone; counters, Auras, or Equipment it had on the battlefield don't count ([Phyrexian Ingester ruling #1]), and only characteristic-defining abilities that define power/toughness apply in exile ([Phyrexian Ingester ruling #2]).
- Layer-wise, Phyrexian Ingester's printed 3/3 is the starting point (rule 302.4c) and the +X/+Y is a modifying effect applied in layer 7c ([613.4c]), so the result is 5/5 with Scarwood Goblins exiled.
- Hypothetically, if some Bird-based effect *did* cause the Imprint ability to trigger twice and both Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant were exiled, [Traveling Chocobo ruling #8] tells you the values for "the exiled card" are summed, giving +5/+5 for an 8/8. That isn't the case here.

This works the same at any number of players; nothing here depends on the player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.607.3: If, within a pair of linked abilities, one ability refers to a single object as “the exiled card,” “a card exiled with [this object],” or a similar phrase, and the other ability has exiled multiple cards (usually because it was copied), the ability refers to each of the exiled cards. If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. If these answers are used to determine the value of a variable, the sum of the answers is used. If that ability performs any actions on “the” card, it performs that action on each exiled card. If that ability creates a token that is a copy of “the” card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card. If that ability performs any actions on “a” card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected.

cited_text.302.4c: Power and toughness are characteristics only creatures have. To determine a creature’s power and toughness, start with the numbers printed in its lower right corner, then apply any applicable continuous effects. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects.”)
cited_text.613.4c: Within layer 7, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order. (See rule 613.7.) Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.) Layer 7c: Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness (but don’t set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value) are applied.

answer_gold:
It's an 8/8.

The enter-the-battlefield ability of Phyrexian Ingester is part of a pair of linked abilities. When determining a value for Phyrexian Ingester's second ability, the sum of the powers and toughnesses from Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant is used. This gives Phyrexian Ingester +5/+5, which makes it an 8/8.

question: Beverly controls [Pandemonium]. Adalynn casts [Knight Errant] and targets Beverly's [Forest Bear] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Channing casts [Ral's Outburst] targeting Adalynn causing them to lose the game. Will Beverly's creature die?
answer:
Direct answer: Beverly's Forest Bear most likely survives, because the player who has to make the Pandemonium choice (Adalynn) is gone; and even in the reading where the damage happens, it would be exactly 2 damage to a 2/2, which would destroy Forest Bear. The provided rules don't fully settle which of those two outcomes applies, so here's the breakdown.

What's certain from the provided material:

- The Pandemonium trigger is controlled by Beverly, not Adalynn, even though Knight Errant entered under Adalynn's control: "If player A controls Pandemonium when a creature enters under player B's control, player A controls the triggered ability even though player B chooses the target and chooses whether to have the creature deal damage" [Pandemonium ruling #1]. So Adalynn losing the game does not remove the ability from the stack — its controller, Beverly, is still in the game.
- Adalynn does lose the game from Ral's Outburst's damage (an effect/damage causing loss; see [104.3e] for effect-based losses), and Knight Errant leaves the game along with Adalynn.
- Knight Errant's power is not locked in until the Pandemonium ability resolves, and if Knight Errant is no longer on the battlefield, the ability uses its power immediately before it left — 2 [Pandemonium ruling #0]. So the damage amount would be 2, which is lethal to Beverly's 2/2 Forest Bear.

The unresolved piece: Pandemonium says "that creature's controller may have it deal damage," and per [Pandemonium ruling #1] that choice belongs to Knight Errant's controller, Adalynn. Adalynn is no longer in the game when the ability resolves, so there is no player available to make that optional choice, which means in practice no damage is dealt and Forest Bear survives. The rules given here don't include a rule telling us what happens to a choice assigned to a player who has left the game, so I can't ground that step further than the ruling itself.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ral's Outburst was cast and resolved while the Pandemonium trigger was still on the stack (as stated, "in response"), and that the target of the trigger was already locked in as Forest Bear when the trigger was put on the stack. If instead the Pandemonium trigger had resolved first, Adalynn would have been present to choose, Knight Errant would have been a 2/2 on the battlefield, and 2 damage to Forest Bear would have destroyed it.

Player count: this is a three-player (or larger) situation with Adalynn, Beverly, and Channing, and it works as described above. Note [801.14] for multiplayer wins/losses; in a two-player game the question couldn't arise as posed since a player leaving would end the game.

answer_gold: The triggered ability of Pandemonium includes a choice to be made upon resolution. However the player that is supposed to make that choice is no longer in the game, therefore the controller of the trigger chooses another player to make that choice. In this case Beverly will choose another player to decide whether Pandemonium's trigger will deal damage to Forest Bear. Beverly is the controller of the trigger since they control the enchantment that generated the trigger, even though Adalynn is the player making choices about the trigger.

question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
answer:
Yes — Asher chooses the color for Hall of Triumph after every player has already chosen which card they're putting onto the battlefield, so Asher knows what Noa is putting in.

How the resolution unfolds:

1. During Show and Tell's resolution, each player chooses a card from their hand — Asher (the active player) first, then the other players in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #2], [101.4b]. A player need not reveal the card, but it must be clear which card was chosen.
2. Only after all those card choices are made are the choices required by the entering permanents themselves made, again in turn order starting with Asher [Show and Tell ruling #0].
3. Hall of Triumph's "As Hall of Triumph enters, choose a color" is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield, and its required choice is made before Hall of Triumph is actually on the battlefield [614.12a].
4. The cards are then put onto the battlefield simultaneously [Show and Tell ruling #2].

So Asher picks the color knowing Noa's card identity. One limit: if Noa's card also requires an "as it enters" choice, Asher must still make Hall of Triumph's color choice first, before Noa announces that choice — Asher knows the card, not the choice for it [Show and Tell ruling #0].

Multiplayer note: this works the same with more than two players; every player chooses a card in turn order first, then the as-enters choices are made in turn order starting with the active player, so Asher knows all players' cards [101.4b], [Show and Tell ruling #0].

Then any appropriate replacement effects, whether they come from that object or from elsewhere, are applied to that event. If a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield requires a choice, that choice is made before the permanent enters the battlefield.

Then the actions happen simultaneously. This rule is often referred to as the “Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) order” rule. A player knows the choices made by the previous players when making their choice, except as specified in 101.4a.

answer_gold: Yes. Show and Tell puts both permanents onto the battlefield at the same time. Before they change zones, both players look at each card.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste).

Why: both effects are ability-adding/ability-removing effects applied in layer 6 [613.1f], and within a layer they're ordered by timestamp, with the later one winning [613.7a], [613.9]. Fleetfeather Sandals grants "Equipped creature has flying and haste"; Tightening Coils says "Enchanted creature gets -6/-0 and loses flying." Originally Tightening Coils had the later timestamp, so Wandering Ones lost flying. When Adriel activates Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability and it resolves, Fleetfeather Sandals becomes attached anew and its continuous effect receives a new (now latest) timestamp [613.7a]. Applying layer 6 in timestamp order, the loss of flying from Tightening Coils is applied first and the grant from Fleetfeather Sandals last, so flying sticks. This matches Tightening Coils ruling #0: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Note that re-attaching Fleetfeather Sandals to the creature it's already on is a legal equip activation targeting a creature Adriel controls [702.6d], [604.4], [301.5f]. The -6/-0 from Tightening Coils is a power/toughness effect in a different layer and is unaffected — Wandering Ones is a -5/1 flier with haste, which still survives (toughness 1) even though its power is negative.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
answer:
Extractor Demon survives. Reality Ripple makes Extractor Demon phase out, and phasing out is not leaving the battlefield, so unearth's "if it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead" replacement never applies [702.84a]. While phased out, Reality Ripple's own text says Extractor Demon "is treated as though it doesn't exist," so at the beginning of the next end step the unearth delayed triggered ability finds nothing to exile — a delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object does nothing if that object isn't there to be affected when it resolves [603.7c]. Extractor Demon then phases in before Addilynn's next untap step and remains on the battlefield with no further exile clause hanging over it, since that delayed ability was one-shot and already resolved.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the question as Reality Ripple resolving before the beginning of the end step, as stated. If instead the unearth delayed trigger had already resolved (or Reality Ripple resolved after that trigger was put on the stack and resolved), Extractor Demon would simply have been exiled at that end step and Reality Ripple would have had no legal target left.

One caveat: the rules excerpt provided here does not include the full phasing rules (702.26), so the "treated as though it doesn't exist" part of this answer rests on Reality Ripple's own printed reminder text rather than a numbered phasing rule. Card text governs over a general rule where they conflict.

Nothing here depends on player count — this works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
answer:
Yes — Natalie's Verity Circle triggers.

Why: Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance, so declaring it as an attacker doesn't tap it (508.1f says attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped, but vigilance prevents that). Koskun Falls' restriction is a mana cost — "pays {2} for each creature they control that's attacking you" — not a "tap a creature" cost. Avery determines and locks in that total cost during the declare attackers step (508.1h), and because the cost requires mana, Avery then gets a chance to activate mana abilities (508.1i, 118.2). Tapping Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher for its {T}: Add {C} equal to its toughness ability is that mana ability; the {C} produced can pay the generic {2} demanded by Koskun Falls, since generic mana can be paid with colorless mana, and paying an attack cost isn't casting a spell from hand, so Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's restriction doesn't apply.

So Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher changes from untapped to tapped by a mana ability, not by being declared as an attacker. Verity Circle's condition "if it isn't being declared as an attacker" is satisfied, exactly as Verity Circle ruling #2 states: a creature with vigilance that's declared as an attacker and then becomes tapped while attacking does trigger Verity Circle. Natalie may then draw a card. (Verity Circle ruling #1: it must actually go from untapped to tapped — true here.)

Multiplayer note: Koskun Falls only taxes creatures attacking Natalie, so with more than two players the answer is unchanged for Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher attacking Natalie specifically; creatures attacking a different opponent wouldn't owe the {2}, and Verity Circle would only trigger if something else tapped them.

question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains 1 life, and Nico loses no life.

Hopeful Eidolon is a 1/1 with lifelink, so its 1 combat damage to Nico normally does two things: Nico loses 1 life, and Alexandra (the source's controller) gains 1 life [702.15b, 120.3a, 120.3f]. Platinum Emperion says "Your life total can't change," which affects only Nico's life total. That ability doesn't prevent damage; it changes the results of the damage, so the damage is still dealt to Nico but the life-loss result does nothing, while the lifelink life gain for Hopeful Eidolon's controller still happens [Platinum Emperion ruling #3]. Any of Nico's abilities that trigger on damage being dealt to Nico would still trigger, since damage was dealt [Platinum Emperion ruling #4].

The reverse case is worth noting: if Nico controlled the creature with lifelink and dealt damage to another player, that player would lose life but Nico would gain none [Platinum Emperion ruling #3].

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; Platinum Emperion only locks its own controller's life total, so the attacking player's life gain is unaffected regardless of table size. (In a Two-Headed Giant-style shared-life game, gaining and losing life still happens per player and is applied to the team total [810.9g].)

One timing note: I'm assuming Hopeful Eidolon was cast as a creature and attacked, dealing combat damage itself. If instead it were cast for its bestow cost as an Aura, it wouldn't be attacking; the enchanted creature would get +1/+1 and lifelink, and that creature's controller would gain the life.

Yes. Damage can have 0 or more results. Normally a creature with lifelink dealing damage to a player would have two results:

* Its controller gains that much life.
* The recipient of the damage loses that much life.

Platinum Emperion makes the second result impossible, so only the first occurs.

question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?
answer:
No. The combat damage from Hero of Oxid Ridge won't be prevented.

Hallow says "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn." It creates a prevention shield tied to the source Nixon chose — the Hero of Oxid Ridge *spell* on the stack. A prevention effect is a continuous "shield" that isn't locked in ahead of time; when damage would actually be dealt, the shield rechecks the source's properties, and if they no longer match, the damage isn't prevented and the shield isn't used up [615.1a] [609.7b] [615.9].

Once the Hero of Oxid Ridge spell resolves it is no longer a spell — it's a creature permanent on the battlefield. So when that 4/2 creature deals combat damage, the source no longer matches "target spell," and Hallow prevents nothing (and Nixon gains no life, since life gain is equal to damage prevented, which is 0) [609.7b] [615.9]. Hallow is essentially wasted here: a creature spell like Hero of Oxid Ridge deals no damage while it's a spell.

Also note Hero of Oxid Ridge's attack triggers still work normally — battle cry pumps Ari's other attackers, and creatures with power 1 or less can't block, checked when blockers are declared [Hero of Oxid Ridge ruling #0]. Nothing about the failed prevention changes that; since the damage isn't prevented, any "deals damage" triggers will still trigger [603.2g].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, except that in multiplayer a prevention effect only applies to sources and recipients within its controller's range of influence [801.13b].

Such effects watch for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevent the damage that would be dealt. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. question: Ariel wants to participate in a sanctioned Magic tournament, but doesn't know where to find one. To which section of the comprehensive rules should they refer?
answer: Ariel should refer to rule 100.6 (specifically 100.6b), the section on tournaments in the Comprehensive Rules. That rule states that players can use the Magic Store & Event Locator at Locator.Wizards.com to find tournaments in their area. Rule 100.6/100.6b also notes that sanctioned tournaments — organized play activities where players compete for prizes — have additional rules covered in the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules, found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents, which may limit the use of some cards, including barring all cards from some older sets. If Ariel is interested in multiplayer tournament play, rule 800.3 adds that many multiplayer Magic tournaments have further rules, including deck construction rules, in that same Tournament Rules document.

question: Ariel controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Nora controls [Kaslem's Strider] enchanted with [Spirit Away]. Ariel casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Spirit Away. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
answer:
Ariel ends up controlling Spirit Away (with no abilities), and Nora gets Kaslem's Strider back as a plain 5/5 with no flying and no +2/+2.

Details:

1) Spirit Away is a legal target. Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Nora's Aura Spirit Away is an artifact permanent an opponent controls, satisfying Opportunistic Dragon's "choose target Human or artifact an opponent controls." (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3 confirms Auras become artifacts; ruling #1 confirms this applies only to permanents on the battlefield, which Spirit Away is. Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2 also makes Spirit Away colorless.) Note that Mycosynth Lattice alone does not make Spirit Away a creature — that requires something like March of the Machines — so the unattach/graveyard outcome in Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3 does not happen here.

2) When Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability resolves, Ariel gains control of Spirit Away, Spirit Away loses all abilities, and Spirit Away can't attack or block (irrelevant for a noncreature). This lasts for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield (Opportunistic Dragon ruling #1).

3) Because Spirit Away has lost all abilities, it no longer has "You control enchanted creature" or "Enchanted creature gets +2/+2 and has flying." Control-changing effects are applied in layer 2 (613.1b), and with Spirit Away's control-change ability gone there is no longer any effect granting control of Kaslem's Strider to anyone else, so Kaslem's Strider is controlled by Nora, its owner. It is a 5/5 Artifact Creature — Golem with no flying and no bonus.

4) Spirit Away physically remains attached to Kaslem's Strider under Ariel's control; the provided rules don't include the attachment-legality state-based action, but nothing in the given rules moves it. It gives no benefit while it has no abilities.

Timing caveat: this assumes Opportunistic Dragon is still on the battlefield when its enters-trigger resolves. If Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield first, per Opportunistic Dragon ruling #3 Nora keeps control of Spirit Away, Spirit Away keeps its abilities, and Nora therefore still controls Kaslem's Strider as a 7/7 flyer — Ariel gains nothing.

Multiplayer: the outcome is the same at any table size; Opportunistic Dragon just targets a permanent controlled by any one opponent Ariel chooses. The multiplayer rules provided here (players leaving the game) would only matter if a player left — e.g., if Ariel left the game, Opportunistic Dragon's control effect would end and Spirit Away would revert to Nora, restoring her control of Kaslem's Strider (800.4a).

question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can legally target Pristine Angel with Mob, even after Pristine Angel becomes untapped.

Why: Pristine Angel's ability only gives it protection "as long as this creature is untapped" — protection from artifacts and from each color. Normally that would stop a black spell like Mob from targeting it once it's untapped. But Cephalid Snitch's ability ("Sacrifice this creature: Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn") already resolved on Pristine Angel earlier in the turn, and that effect lasts until end of turn. It removes protection from black for the rest of the turn regardless of how many times Pristine Angel taps and untaps, so when Atlas untaps it with the "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" trigger, the protection ability grants everything except protection from black.

Mob is a mono-black instant ({4}{B}) and not an artifact, so nothing about Pristine Angel's remaining protections (from artifacts and from the other four colors) stops it. Mob's target is legal on announcement and still legal on resolution, so Pristine Angel is destroyed unless something else intervenes.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved during this same turn, before Atlas cast the spell that untapped Pristine Angel — that's how the question reads. If instead Cephalid Snitch's ability had been used on a previous turn, the "until end of turn" effect would have expired and untapped Pristine Angel would again have protection from black, making it an illegal target for Mob.

A couple of side notes: this all happens after combat, and untapping a creature that was declared as an attacker never removes it from combat anyway (506.4b). If Nico uses convoke to help pay for Mob, tapping creatures for convoke doesn't change Mob's mana cost or mana value, and Nico may tap even creatures he hasn't controlled since the start of his most recent turn (Mob rulings #2 and #5). Nothing here depends on the player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

answer_gold: Yes. "Protection from all colors" means the same thing as an individual protection ability for each color, so Pristine Angel will lose protection from black while still having protection from all other colors and from artifacts.

question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
No — Gaea's Liege can't be declared as an attacker attacking Naomi herself.

Why: Bayou has the basic land type Forest ([Bayou ruling #0], [Bayou ruling #1]). Ashley controls 1 Forest, so while Gaea's Liege isn't attacking it's 1/1. When you declare attackers you use the "not attacking" power and toughness — it only changes after declaration is complete ([Gaea's Liege ruling #0]). So at the moment of declaration Gaea's Liege has power 1, and Reverence's "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you" is a restriction that makes declaring it as an attacker against Naomi illegal ([508.1c], [802.3a]). The fact that it would become 3/3 (Naomi's 3 Bayous) once attacking doesn't matter; the restriction is checked at declaration.

Exceptions/other legal targets:
- If Naomi controls a planeswalker, Gaea's Liege may attack that planeswalker — a creature that can't attack you can still attack a planeswalker you control ([Reverence ruling #0], [802.3a]). Same for a battle Naomi protects ([310.5], [310.8b]).
- In a multiplayer game, Reverence only protects Naomi. Ashley can freely attack any other opponent within her range of influence (or their planeswalkers/battles) with Gaea's Liege ([801.3], [802.3a]); if the table uses attack-left/attack-right, Ashley's legal defenders are limited accordingly ([803.1a]). With exactly two players (Ashley and Naomi), and no planeswalker or battle available, Gaea's Liege simply can't attack this turn.
- Also note the usual requirements: Gaea's Liege must be untapped and have haste or have been under Ashley's control since the turn began ([508.1a]).
- If instead an effect merely put Gaea's Liege onto the battlefield attacking or stated it is attacking, restrictions like Reverence's wouldn't apply, since such a creature isn't affected by declaration-time restrictions ([508.4c]).

question: Arjun's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
answer:
Arjun chooses the order. When Morality Shift resolves, the cards from Arjun's library all go to Arjun's graveyard at the same time, and as the owner of those cards Arjun may arrange them in any order they like ([404.3], and Morality Shift's own ruling that "You can choose the order of the cards being placed into the graveyard").

Details:
- Morality Shift reads "Exchange your graveyard and library. Then shuffle your library." So the old graveyard becomes the new library (and is then shuffled, so its order is irrelevant), while the old library becomes the new graveyard.
- Because an effect is putting two or more cards into the same graveyard simultaneously, [404.3] lets Arjun, the owner, arrange them in any order. The graveyard is a single face-up pile that normally can't be reordered afterward ([404.2]), so this is Arjun's one chance to set that order.
- No opponent has any input, and Morality Shift works even if Arjun's graveyard or library is empty (Morality Shift ruling #1).
- This doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since only Arjun makes the choice. (If several players somehow had to make such choices at once, APNAP order in [101.4] would govern who chooses first.)

question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?
answer:
One black mana — {B} — is produced. Ares taps Gaea's Cradle for mana, and Nico's Contamination replaces what that land produces.

Why: Gaea's Cradle's ability reads "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." With no creatures, on its own it would add no mana. It is still a mana ability regardless [605.2], and "tapping for mana" simply means activating a mana ability that includes {T} in its cost [106.12b]. Contamination's second ability is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability [Contamination ruling #0], and its printed text says "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount." Because that text explicitly overrides both the type and the amount, the {G}-for-each-creature amount (zero) is replaced with exactly one {B}; the card's own text controls over the general expectation that a zero-mana ability yields nothing. Note also Contamination affects color and amount from the land itself, while separate external mana-doubling type effects are handled per [Contamination ruling #2].

One caveat on grounding: [106.12b] describes a replacement effect as modifying the mana production event "while such an ability is resolving and producing mana," which some read as requiring at least some mana to exist to be replaced; under that stricter reading nothing would be produced. The plain wording of Contamination ("instead of any other type and amount") is the more specific instruction and wins, so {B} is produced.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer: Contamination isn't limited to its controller's opponents — it applies to every land tapped for mana by any player, so Nico's own lands are likewise restricted to {B}.

See rule 605, “Mana Abilities.” A replacement effect that applies if a permanent “is tapped for mana” or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.

A permanent has an ability that reads “{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control.” The ability is still a mana ability even if you control no creatures or if the permanent is already tapped.

question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
answer:
Yes — Aubrey loses 1 life when Necromancy is sacrificed at the beginning of the next cleanup step, because Necromancy is a nontoken card being put into Aubrey's (an opponent of Nikolai's) graveyard during that same turn.

Why: Necromancy was cast during Aubrey's declare blockers step, i.e., a time a sorcery couldn't be cast, so its own text makes "the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step." That sacrifice happens in the cleanup step of the same turn, and Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability sets up a delayed trigger that watches for cards put into an opponent's graveyard "this turn" (Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0). Effects that last for the turn don't expire when the end step ends — only effects worded to last until the end of that step do (500.5), and the cleanup step is still part of the same turn. Sacrificing means Aubrey moves Necromancy from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard (701.21a, Sacrifice), so a card is indeed put into a graveyard, and Aubrey loses 1 life (119.3).

Timing note/assumption: I'm assuming Nikolai's activation resolved during Aubrey's end step, before the cleanup step (as stated). If it somehow failed to resolve before the sacrifice, no trigger would exist to see the sacrifice and Aubrey would lose nothing.

Extras worth knowing:
- Necromancy's leave-the-battlefield clause also makes the reanimated creature's controller sacrifice it. If that creature is a nontoken card owned by an opponent of Nikolai, that's another instance of Duskmantle Guildmage's delayed trigger and another 1 life lost; if it were a token, it wouldn't trigger at all (Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #1). Leaves-the-battlefield-style triggers do "look back in time" (603.10a).
- If Nikolai activated the ability more than once, each resolution creates a separate delayed trigger, so each card hitting Aubrey's graveyard costs 1 life per instance (Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0).
- Multiplayer: Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability considers all of Nikolai's opponents, not just one (Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #2), so the answer is the same at a bigger table — Aubrey loses the life as Necromancy's controller/owner, and any other opponent's cards hitting their graveyard that turn would also cost them life.
- Note the sacrifice clause only applies because Necromancy was cast with its own flash-granting ability; if some other effect had allowed the flash-speed cast, there'd be no cleanup-step sacrifice at all (Necromancy ruling #4).

question: Alma casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Nico's [Bronze Sable]. In response, Nico casts [Brute Strength] on the Bronze Sable. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
At end of the turn Bronze Sable dies, and Nico gets a poison counter from Virulent Wound.

Step by step:

1. Nico's Brute Strength resolves first (it was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack), giving Bronze Sable +3/+1 and trample until end of turn. Bronze Sable is 2/1 printed, so it becomes 5/2.
2. Alma's Virulent Wound then resolves and puts a -1/-1 counter on Bronze Sable. Counters and continuous power/toughness effects are all applied in layer 7 [613.1g], so Bronze Sable is 2/1 base, +3/+1 from Brute Strength, -1/-1 from the counter = 4/1. It survives with toughness 1 or more, so it isn't destroyed at this time [704.5f].
3. When the turn ends, the "until end of turn" effect from Brute Strength expires [500.5a]. The -1/-1 counter is a permanent counter and does not go away. Bronze Sable is now 2/1 with a -1/-1 counter = 1/0.
4. Toughness 0 is a state-based action: Bronze Sable is put into Nico's graveyard immediately, with no player getting priority first, and regeneration can't save it [704.5f].
5. Virulent Wound's delayed trigger — "When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter" — is still watching for that death, and Bronze Sable did die during this same turn, so it triggers and Nico gets one poison counter. Had Bronze Sable survived past the turn, no poison counter would be given [Virulent Wound ruling #0].

Timing note: I've assumed the normal stack order (Brute Strength resolving before Virulent Wound, since it was cast in response). If instead Virulent Wound had already resolved before Brute Strength was cast, the outcome is the same — Bronze Sable would be 1/0 momentarily and would die immediately upon Virulent Wound resolving, and Nico would get the poison counter right away rather than at end of turn.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Angelina controls [Ice Cauldron]. Noel controls [Suppression Field]. Angelina activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Angelina's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
answer:
Angelina adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana — spendable only to cast the card exiled with Ice Cauldron.

Why: Ice Cauldron's first ability is an activated ability that is not a mana ability (it exiles a card and puts a charge counter on Ice Cauldron; it doesn't produce mana), so Suppression Field's "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities" applies. With X=1, the total activation cost became {1} + {2} = {3} generic plus {T}, which Angelina paid with {C}{C}{C}.

Ice Cauldron notes "the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost" — the actual mana paid, not the value of X. Per [Ice Cauldron ruling #8], Ice Cauldron counts only the mana actually spent and doesn't see X or cost adjustments, so the noted mana is {C}{C}{C}, all three colorless mana, including the portion that covered Suppression Field's tax.

On the later turn, Ice Cauldron's second ability ("{T}, Remove a charge counter: Add this artifact's last noted type and amount of mana") is a mana ability — it produces mana ([Ice Cauldron ruling #0]) — so Suppression Field does not tax it ([Suppression Field ruling #0]). Angelina pays only {T} and removing the charge counter, and adds {C}{C}{C}. That mana is restricted to casting the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron; the restriction doesn't change the mana's type ([106.6]), and Angelina may add other mana to finish paying the spell's cost ([Ice Cauldron ruling #5]).

Note that {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic — it can pay generic costs but a {C} in a cost can't be paid with colored mana.

This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer table: Suppression Field affects all activated abilities regardless of controller, and Noel controlling it is irrelevant to whether the tax applies.

An ability’s activation cost must be paid by the player who is activating it. The activation cost of an ability that reads “{2}, {T}: You gain 1 life” is two mana of any type plus tapping the permanent that has the ability.
gold_text.602.2b: To activate an ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an object’s controller (or its owner, if it doesn’t have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. Activating an ability follows the steps listed below, in order. If, at any point during the activation of an ability, a player is unable to comply with any of those steps, the activation is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Announcements and payments can’t be altered after they’ve been made. The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2b–i. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated ability’s analog to a spell’s mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.
