question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm, but only before finishing the search, and they must pay {5}{G}{G}.

Why: Panglacial Wurm says "While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library." Aven Mindcensor replaces Ariel's search of their library with searching only the top four cards of that library, but that still counts as searching that library for effects that care ([Aven Mindcensor ruling #0], [701.23f]), so Panglacial Wurm's ability is active. Aven Mindcensor's restriction also means Ariel may only look at (and only find) those top four cards ([Aven Mindcensor ruling #2]) — since Panglacial Wurm is among them here, it's visible and castable. If it had been the fifth card or deeper, Ariel could not have cast it, because they can't look at it at all.

Timing and mechanics:
- Ariel must cast Panglacial Wurm before finding any card with Warped Landscape's search ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #1]).
- Casting follows all normal rules except timing and zone; it goes on the stack, and Ariel pays {5}{G}{G} (five generic plus two green), and may activate mana abilities while doing so ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #0]).
- Panglacial Wurm cast this way can't then be found by Warped Landscape's search ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #4]) — which doesn't matter much, since Warped Landscape only finds a basic land card anyway.
- After casting, Ariel resumes the search, gets a basic land onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffles the entire library (the whole library shuffles, not just the top four — [Aven Mindcensor ruling #1], [701.23f]). When Warped Landscape's ability finishes resolving, the active player gets priority with Panglacial Wurm on the stack ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #3]).

Assumed timing: Aven Mindcensor resolved before Warped Landscape's ability, as stated, so its replacement effect applies to this search. If Aven Mindcensor had instead resolved after the search was already underway, it wouldn't affect that search.

This all works identically at a two-player or multiplayer table: Aven Mindcensor affects any opponent's library search, and Panglacial Wurm only works while its controller searches their own library ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #6]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.6: If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
gold_text.701.23f: Search If searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Any abilities that trigger on a library being searched will trigger. Aven Mindcensor says, in part, “If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead.” Veteran Explorer says “When this creature dies, each player may search their library for up to two basic land cards, put them onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” An opponent who searched the top four cards of their library because of Veteran Explorer’s ability would shuffle the entire library.

cited_text.701.23f: Search If searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Any abilities that trigger on a library being searched will trigger. Aven Mindcensor says, in part, “If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead.” Veteran Explorer says “When this creature dies, each player may search their library for up to two basic land cards, put them onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” An opponent who searched the top four cards of their library because of Veteran Explorer’s ability would shuffle the entire library.

answer_gold: Yes. Aven Mindcensor's ability is a replacement effect that replaces searching a library with searching only the top four cards of that library. However for the purposes of Panglacial Wurm's effect, it still qualifies as "searching a library".

question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
The sideboard card Addison brought into the game with Glittering Wish stays in the game and becomes part of Addison's library for the new game.

Details:

- Glittering Wish let Addison reveal a multicolored card they own from outside the game and put it into their hand (in a tournament that card comes from Addison's sideboard — [Glittering Wish ruling #0]). "Outside the game" isn't a zone; a card is outside the game if it isn't in any of the game's zones [400.11a].
- When Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, the old game immediately ends with no one winning, losing, or drawing, and all players still in it begin a new game following the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1] [104.6] [Karn Liberated ruling #12].
- Crucially, every card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, "even if those cards were not originally involved in the restarted game," and a card brought in from outside the game will be part of that player's library when the new game begins [727.2]. So the wished-for card shuffles into Addison's starting deck rather than going back to the sideboard — it does not matter what zone it was in (battlefield, graveyard, exile) when the restart happened. Glittering Wish itself, which exiled itself on resolution and is now in the graveyard per the question's description, likewise joins Addison's library and is shuffled in.
- The only exception is cards exempted from the restart procedure, which are not in their owner's deck as the new game begins [727.5] — for Karn Liberated that means non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 abilities, which stay in exile and are then put onto the battlefield under Karn Liberated's controller's control [Karn Liberated ruling #6] [Karn Liberated ruling #4]. Glittering Wish is a sorcery and was exiled by its own effect, not by Karn Liberated, so it gets no such exemption.
- Addison cannot swap the wished card back out: players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5]. Addison is the starting player in the new game, everyone shuffles, resets to the starting life total, draws seven, and may mulligan [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving just before the first untap step, with any resulting triggers going on the stack in the first upkeep step [727.4] [Karn Liberated ruling #4].
- Number of players: this works the same with two players or more. In a multiplayer game, any player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11], and if a player leaves, all cards they own leave with them [Karn Liberated ruling #3].

Timing note: I'm assuming the wish resolved and the fetched card entered the game before Karn Liberated's −14 resolved. If instead the card had never actually been brought into the game (e.g., Glittering Wish was countered), it would still be outside the game and simply remain in the sideboard, set aside during the new game's pregame procedure [103.2a].

Ownership of cards in the new game doesn’t change, regardless of their location when the new game begins. A player casts Living Wish, bringing a creature card into the game from outside the game. After this happens, each player’s deck is considered their starting deck.

answer_gold: The sideboard card is shuffled into Addison's library for the restarted game.

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the Copy Artifact permanent stops being a Dance of the Dead entirely and becomes a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm (a 6/4 Wurm, colorless and an artifact because of Mycosynth Lattice) that keeps only the {1}{U}{R} Mizzium Transreliquat ability. Because it is no longer an Aura, it becomes unattached from Viashino Warrior, but it never left the battlefield, so Dance of the Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability never triggers — and that ability is gone anyway. Viashino Warrior simply stays on the battlefield under Alvin's control as a 4/2 (it loses the +1/+1 and the "doesn't untap" restriction), still tapped, since a permanent keeps its tapped status until something changes it [110.5c].

Why each step works:

1. Copy Artifact entered as a copy of Mizzium Transreliquat. Copy effects already applying to Mizzium Transreliquat are copied, so Copy Artifact's copiable values were those of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} "becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability, plus Copy Artifact's own exception making it an enchantment in addition to its other types [707.3], [707.9a], [707.9b], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0].

2. Sakashima of a Thousand Faces's "enter as a copy of another creature you control" is an as-enters choice, and choices aren't copied — Copy Artifact's controller makes it fresh [707.6]. Dance of the Dead was a legal choice because Mycosynth Lattice made it an artifact and March of the Machines made that noncreature artifact an artifact creature [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1], [March of the Machines].

3. An Aura that is also a creature can't enchant anything and is unattached and put into the graveyard as state-based actions [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3] — but state-based actions aren't performed during a spell's resolution, and March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked before Eureka finished, so by the time the game checked, the Copy Artifact/Dance of the Dead was not a creature and stayed legally attached. Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked entered with one +1/+1 counter. Dance of the Dead's enters trigger waited until Eureka finished resolving [Eureka ruling #3].

4. Activating {1}{U}{R} targeting Streetbreaker Wurm is legal because Mycosynth Lattice makes Streetbreaker Wurm an artifact. That new copy effect overwrites all previous copiable values, so the permanent loses the Dance of the Dead text, the Sakashima abilities, and the "also an enchantment" modification; it keeps only the granted {1}{U}{R} ability, and this does not wear off at end of turn [707.3], [707.9b], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #4]. Non-copy effects like Mycosynth Lattice's type/color changes still apply on top [707.4].

5. Note the real Mizzium Transreliquat is still a Sakashima of a Thousand Faces copy, so the "legend rule" still doesn't apply to Alvin's permanents [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #0], [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #6].

6. The new Streetbreaker Wurm copy hasn't been controlled as a creature since Alvin's turn began in the usual sense; treat it as subject to summoning sickness for attacking and {T} abilities [March of the Machines ruling #4].

Timing assumption: I assumed the sacrifice of March of the Machines happened during Eureka's resolution (as stated) and thus before any state-based action check. If March of the Machines were still on the battlefield when state-based actions were next checked, the Copy Artifact/Dance of the Dead would have been an Aura creature, become unattached, and be put into its owner's graveyard, and its enters trigger would have done nothing (no legally enchanted card), so Viashino Warrior would never have returned.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players except that Eureka's loop goes around all players and ends only after every player in sequence declines [Eureka ruling #0]; the outcome for Alvin's permanents is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

gold_text.613.1: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order:
gold_text.704.5m: The state-based actions are as follows: If an Aura is attached to an illegal object or player, or is not attached to an object or player, that Aura is put into its owner’s graveyard.
gold_text.704.5p: The state-based actions are as follows: If a battle or creature is attached to an object or player, it becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield. Similarly, if any nonbattle, noncreature permanent that’s neither an Aura, an Equipment, nor a Fortification is attached to an object or player, it becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield.

cited_text.110.5c: A permanent’s status is its physical state. There are four status categories, each of which has two possible values: tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, face up/face down, and phased in/phased out. Each permanent always has one of these values for each of these categories. A permanent retains its status until a spell, ability, or turn-based action changes it, even if that status is not relevant to it. Dimir Doppelganger says “{1}{U}{B}: Exile target creature card from a graveyard. This creature becomes a copy of that card, except it has this ability.” It becomes a copy of Jushi Apprentice, a flip card. Through use of Jushi Apprentice’s ability, this creature flips, making it a copy of Tomoya the Revealer with the Dimir Doppelganger ability. If this permanent then becomes a copy of Runeclaw Bear, it will retain its flipped status even though that has no relevance to Runeclaw Bear. If its copy ability is activated again, this time targeting a Nezumi Shortfang card (another flip card), this permanent’s flipped status means it will have the characteristics of Stabwhisker the Odious (the flipped version of Nezumi Shortfang) with the Dimir Doppelganger ability.
cited_text.707.3: The copy’s copiable values become the copied information, as modified by the copy’s status (see rule 110.5). Objects that copy the object will use the new copiable values. Vesuvan Doppelganger reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield, except it doesn’t copy that creature’s color and it has ‘At the beginning of your upkeep, you may have this creature become a copy of target creature, except it doesn’t copy that creature’s color and it has this ability.’” A Vesuvan Doppelganger enters the battlefield as a copy of Runeclaw Bear (a 2/2 green Bear creature with no abilities). Then a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of the Doppelganger. The Clone is a 2/2 blue Bear named Runeclaw Bear that has the Doppelganger’s upkeep-triggered ability. Tomoya the Revealer (a flipped flip card) becomes a copy of Nezumi Shortfang (an unflipped flip card). Tomoya’s characteristics become the characteristics of Stabwhisker the Odious, which is the flipped version of Nezumi Shortfang. A face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph) becomes a copy of a face-up Branchsnap Lorian (a 4/1 green creature with trample and morph {G}). The Demon’s characteristics become the characteristics of Branchsnap Lorian. However, since the creature is face down, it remains a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities, and no mana cost. It can be turned face up for {G}. If it’s turned face up, it will have the characteristics of Branchsnap Lorian. A face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph) becomes a copy of Wandering Ones (a 1/1 blue Spirit creature that doesn’t have morph). It will be a face-down Wandering Ones. It remains a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities, and no mana cost. Its controller can’t turn it face up as a special action. If an effect turns it face up, it will have the characteristics of Wandering Ones.
cited_text.707.4: Some effects cause a permanent that’s copying a permanent to copy a different object while remaining on the battlefield. The change doesn’t cause enters-the-battlefield or leaves-the-battlefield abilities to trigger. This also doesn’t change any noncopy effects presently affecting the permanent. Unstable Shapeshifter reads, “Whenever another creature enters, this creature becomes a copy of that creature, except it has this ability.” It’s affected by Giant Growth, which reads “Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn.” If a creature enters the battlefield later this turn, Unstable Shapeshifter will become a copy of that creature, but it will still get +3/+3 from the Giant Growth.
cited_text.707.6: When copying a permanent, any choices that have been made for that permanent aren’t copied. Instead, if an object enters the battlefield as a copy of another permanent, the object’s controller will get to make any “as [this] enters the battlefield” choices for it. A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Adaptive Automaton. Adaptive Automaton reads, in part, “As this creature enters, choose a creature type.” The Clone won’t copy the creature type choice of the Automaton; rather, the controller of the Clone will get to make a new choice.
cited_text.707.9a: Copy effects may include modifications or exceptions to the copying process. Some copy effects cause the copy to gain an ability as part of the copying process. This ability becomes part of the copiable values for the copy, along with any other abilities that were copied. Quirion Elves enters the battlefield and an Unstable Shapeshifter copies it. The copiable values of the Shapeshifter now match those of the Elves, except that the Shapeshifter also has the ability “Whenever another creature enters, this creature becomes a copy of that creature, except it has this ability.” Then a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of the Unstable Shapeshifter. The Clone copies the new copiable values of the Shapeshifter, including the ability that the Shapeshifter gave itself when it copied the Elves.
cited_text.707.9b: Copy effects may include modifications or exceptions to the copying process. Some copy effects modify a characteristic as part of the copying process. The final set of values for that characteristic becomes part of the copiable values of the copy. Copy Artifact is an enchantment that reads, “You may have this enchantment enter as a copy of any artifact on the battlefield, except it’s an enchantment in addition to its other types.” It enters the battlefield as a copy of Juggernaut. The copiable values of the Copy Artifact now match those of Juggernaut with one modification: its types are now artifact, creature, and enchantment.

answer_gold: The Copy Artifact becomes unattached from the Viashino Warrior. It still has the ability "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Dance of the Dead", but it's not an Aura so nothing happens to it if it isn't enchanting a legal object. If Copy Artifact leaves the battlefield later, Alvin will have to sacrifice Viashino Warrior.

question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Short answer: Blood Tyrant's "whenever a player loses the game" ability does trigger on Aspen's loss, but it never resolves, so Blood Tyrant gets no +1/+1 counters — and Blood Tyrant reverts to Briella's control.

Why:

1. Volt Charge deals 3 damage to Aspen, who was at 1 life; that damage is processed into life loss [120.4c], so Aspen is at -2 life and loses the game as a state-based action [119.6].

2. Blood Tyrant's third ability ("Whenever a player loses the game, put five +1/+1 counters on this creature") triggers on a loss for any reason, including a state-based action from a life total of 0 or less [Blood Tyrant ruling #1], [603.9]. Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game "look back in time" — the game uses the existence of the abilities and the appearance of objects immediately before the event [603.10f] — so the fact that Aspen is gone afterward doesn't stop the trigger itself, and at that moment Aspen controlled Blood Tyrant via Malevolent Whispers.

3. However, Aspen leaving the game happens immediately, and when a player leaves the game, any objects on the stack that player controlled which aren't represented by cards cease to exist; control-change effects that player created or benefited from end [800.4a]. Malevolent Whispers' control effect ends, so Briella's Blood Tyrant goes back to Briella (Malevolent Whispers itself is Aspen's card and leaves with Aspen). The triggered ability is Aspen's, and it isn't a card on the stack, so it ceases to exist rather than resolving. No +1/+1 counters are ever put on Blood Tyrant.

Player count matters here: with more than two players, the game continues as described above and Briella simply gets Blood Tyrant back with no new counters. In a two‑player game (just Aspen and Cason, with Briella's Blood Tyrant somehow in play), Aspen losing ends the game outright, so counters are moot.

Timing note: I'm assuming Volt Charge fully resolved (damage, then proliferate) before Aspen's life total was checked, since state-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority. If instead you imagine Aspen already at 0 or less before Volt Charge resolved, Aspen would have left the game earlier and Volt Charge would have had an illegal target and not resolved at all — no damage, no proliferate [Volt Charge ruling #0].

Also note Blood Tyrant's own upkeep ability is unrelated here: it only counts life lost from that ability [Blood Tyrant ruling #0].

gold_text.603.10: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.10f: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game look back in time.
gold_text.800.4a: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. Alex casts Mind Control, an Aura that reads, “You control enchanted creature,” on Bianca’s Assault Griffin. If Alex leaves the game, so does Mind Control, and Assault Griffin reverts to Bianca’s control. If, instead, Bianca leaves the game, so does Assault Griffin, and Mind Control is put into Alex’s graveyard. Alex casts Act of Treason, which reads, in part, “Gain control of target creature until end of turn,” targeting Bianca’s Runeclaw Bears. If Alex leaves the game, Act of Treason’s change-of-control effect ends and Runeclaw Bears reverts to Bianca’s control. Alex casts Bribery, which reads, “Search target opponent’s library for a creature card and put that card onto the battlefield under your control. Then that player shuffles their library,” targeting Bianca. Alex puts Serra Angel onto the battlefield from Bianca’s library. If Bianca leaves the game, Serra Angel also leaves the game. If, instead, Alex leaves the game, Serra Angel is exiled. Alex controls Genesis Chamber, which reads, “Whenever a nontoken creature enters, if Genesis Chamber is untapped, that creature’s controller creates a 1/1 colorless Myr artifact creature token.” If Alex leaves the game, all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under Alex’s control leave the game, and all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under any other player’s control remain in the game.

question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
answer:
Yes — Aspen draws a card during their draw step.

Two things make this work. First, this is a multiplayer game, and in multiplayer games no player skips the draw step of their first turn, including the starting player [103.8c]. Second, killing Brycen doesn't end the game: Brycen loses and therefore leaves the game [104.5], but a multiplayer game continues after one or more players have left [800.4k], and Aspen would only win outright if all of Aspen's opponents had left [104.2a] — Collins is still in. So Aspen's turn proceeds normally.

The "upkeep" (upkeep step) comes before the draw step, so the Leyline of Anticipation / Simian Spirit Guide / Desperate Ritual / Goblin Charbelcher kill happens before the draw. Leyline of Anticipation was on the battlefield from the start of the game per its own text and [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0], letting Aspen cast Desperate Ritual as though it had flash during the upkeep step; Simian Spirit Guide's exile-for-{R} ability is a mana ability. Immediately after Aspen's draw step begins, the turn-based action of drawing a card occurs and doesn't use the stack [504.1] [703.4d].

Contrast: in a two-player game, killing your only opponent would end the game immediately [104.2a], so there'd be no draw step at all — and note that the starting player in a two-player game does skip their first draw step. Here, with three players, neither applies. If a triggered ability keys off a player losing the game, it triggers on Brycen leaving [603.9].

question: Addison, Brixton, and Collins started playing a multiplayer game. Collins lost the game, and then Addison restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Addison draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
answer:
No — Addison will skip the draw step of the first turn of the restarted game, so Addison does not draw a card.

Why: Collins had already lost and left the game before the restart, and only players still in the game when it restarts are involved in the new game [104.6][727.1a][Karn Liberated ruling #11]. That means the new game begins with just Addison and Brixton — a two-player game. Addison, as the controller of the ability that restarted the game, is the starting player [727.1a][Karn Liberated ruling #9], and in a two-player game the player who plays first skips their first draw step [103.8a]. The draw would otherwise be a turn-based action at the start of the draw step [703.4d][504.1].

Contrast: if Collins had still been in the game at the moment of the restart, the new game would be a three-player multiplayer game, and then Addison as starting player would NOT skip the draw step [800.7][103.8c] (the only multiplayer exception is Two-Headed Giant, where the team playing first does skip it).

Also note for the first turn: Karn Liberated's −14 finishes resolving just before the first untap step, putting the non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn onto the battlefield under Addison's control, and any resulting triggers go on the stack in the first upkeep step [727.4][Karn Liberated ruling #4]. And any player with fewer than seven cards in their library after drawing seven will lose during that first upkeep step [727.3].

question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?
answer:
No. Nico can't activate the granted ability; only Aniyah can, even while Nico controls Douser of Lights.

Why: Martyrdom grants Douser of Lights the ability "{0}: The next 1 damage that would be dealt to target creature, planeswalker, or player this turn is dealt to this creature instead," plus the instruction "Only you may activate this ability." When an effect adds an activated ability, any activation instructions included in that effect become part of the added ability [113.10a] — so the "only you" restriction (referring to Aniyah, Martyrdom's controller) rides along with the ability on Douser of Lights. A restriction on an activated ability's use continues to apply to the object even if that object's controller changes [602.5b], and a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5, 602.5b]. Act of Aggression only gives Nico control of Douser of Lights until end of turn (untapping it and giving it haste); it doesn't rewrite who "you" means in Martyrdom's grant.

So during the turn, Aniyah — not Nico — remains the only player who may pay {0} and activate that redirection ability, even though Nico is the one controlling Douser of Lights. Note the redirection sends damage to Douser of Lights itself; if Douser of Lights leaves the battlefield or stops being a creature before the redirection applies, the damage stays where it was [Martyrdom ruling #1, Martyrdom ruling #2].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players: whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, the "only you" restriction still limits activation to Aniyah, and Act of Aggression can target a creature any opponent controls [Act of Aggression ruling #5].

question: Ashley has restarted the game with a [Karn Liberated] that exiled an [Ajani's Chosen]. Ashley chooses to begin the restarted game with a [Leyline of Anticipation] on the battlefield. Does Ajani's Chosen trigger?
answer:
No — Ajani's Chosen does not trigger.

Timing is the whole answer. Leyline of Anticipation is put onto the battlefield as part of the pregame procedure, after mulligans are complete ([103.6a], [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0], [Karn Liberated ruling #9]). Karn Liberated's restart effect doesn't finish resolving — and the non-Aura permanent cards it left in exile, including Ajani's Chosen, aren't put onto the battlefield — until after the pregame procedure is complete and just before the first turn's untap step ([727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4]).

So when Leyline of Anticipation enters the battlefield, Ajani's Chosen is still in exile and has no ability on the battlefield to trigger. Ajani's Chosen's ability only triggers on an enchantment entering while Ajani's Chosen is already there ([Ajani's Chosen ruling #3] — the ability doesn't trigger until the enchantment enters the battlefield). Ajani's Chosen entering later does not retroactively see Leyline of Anticipation's earlier entry.

Note for contrast: if Karn Liberated's ability had put an enchantment onto the battlefield at the same time as Ajani's Chosen, any resulting triggers would go on the stack at the beginning of the first upkeep step ([727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4]). Also, Ajani's Chosen will have been under Ashley's control continuously since the beginning of Ashley's first turn ([Karn Liberated ruling #2]).

This works the same with two players or more than two; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that any player who had already left the game before the restart isn't in the new game ([727.7], [Karn Liberated ruling #11]).

question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
answer:
X will equal 3.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a 1/1 with the ability "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is not the hand or library, so when Bishop of Binding exiles Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, its two +1/+1 counters remain on it, and counters that modify power/toughness apply in zones other than the battlefield too — so the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 3/3 [122.1a] [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5].

This is an exception to Bishop of Binding's normal behavior: the ruling that "any counters on the exiled creature will cease to exist" [Bishop of Binding ruling #1] is the general result, but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own printed text specifically overrides that, and card text wins over a general rule it contradicts. Note the counters aren't newly "placed" — they simply persist [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #0].

When Bishop of Binding attacks, its trigger sets X to the power of the exiled card, measured only as that ability resolves [Bishop of Binding ruling #5]. That power is 3, so the target Vampire gets +3/+3 until end of turn. If Bishop of Binding left the battlefield while the ability was on the stack (so Skullbriar, the Walking Grave returned and there is no exiled card), X would instead be 0 [Bishop of Binding ruling #0].

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Ari and Nehemiah's objects are involved.

question: Neriah controls a [Containment Priest] and has a [Knotvine Mystic] in their graveyard. Alan casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Neriah. What happens to the Knotvine Mystic?
answer:
Knotvine Mystic ends up in exile. Ghastly Conscription first exiles Knotvine Mystic from Neriah's graveyard face down, shuffles the pile, and then tries to manifest it — put it onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature. Because that manifested permanent would be a nontoken creature entering the battlefield without having been cast, Containment Priest's replacement ability applies and exiles Knotvine Mystic instead of letting it enter. It never becomes a face-down permanent on the battlefield.

Why the exceptions don't help here: Containment Priest's ability only spares creatures that were actually cast, and Ghastly Conscription's manifest is not a cast [Containment Priest ruling #1]. Also, a manifested card enters as a 2/2 creature [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8], so Knotvine Mystic is entering as a creature and is exiled; the carve-out in [Containment Priest ruling #3] only protects a creature card that would enter as a noncreature permanent. Note that Containment Priest's printed text ("If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead") is what governs here, overriding the normal outcome of the manifest effect.

If Alan's Ghastly Conscription exiles multiple creature cards from Neriah's graveyard, every one of them is exiled by Containment Priest as it tries to enter, so Alan gets nothing from the spell — Ghastly Conscription still resolves and still exiles the cards from the graveyard.

This works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided material is that if Alan later leaves the game, manifested cards he controls that are owned by an opponent are exiled [Ghastly Conscription ruling #6] — moot here since nothing ever hits the battlefield.

question: Avery controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Leatherback Baloth]s with magnet counters on them. Nayeli controls one [Imperial Moth] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nayeli's legal blocks?
answer:
Nayeli must block one of the two Leatherback Baloths with Imperial Moth — her choice which one. Declining to block is illegal, and blocking both is impossible with a single creature.

Why: each Leatherback Baloth attacking with a magnet counter triggers Magnetic Web's second ability, so Nayeli has two separate requirements: "Imperial Moth blocks Leatherback Baloth #1 if able" and "Imperial Moth blocks Leatherback Baloth #2 if able." A requirement is an effect saying a creature must block. Under rule 509.1c, the declaration is illegal only if the number of requirements obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number that could be obeyed without breaking any restriction. Imperial Moth is one untapped creature and can be assigned to only one attacking creature (509.1a), so the maximum obtainable is one requirement — she satisfies the rules by blocking either Leatherback Baloth, and it doesn't matter which. Blocking nothing obeys zero of one possible requirement and is therefore an illegal declaration.

No restriction interferes: neither Leatherback Baloth has an evasion ability (509.1b), and Imperial Moth's flying only matters for what can block it, not what it can block. Imperial Moth is an enchantment creature, which is fine — the only type prohibition in 509.1a is that a blocker can't be a battle.

One timing note: this assumes Imperial Moth already had its magnet counter and was untapped when the declare blockers step began. If Imperial Moth were tapped, or the counter were added after blockers were declared, it wouldn't be able to block and Nayeli would have no legal block to make.

With exactly two players in combat here, Nayeli is the sole defending player. In a multiplayer game, blocks are declared by each defending player in APNAP order, and each defending player may block only creatures attacking them, a planeswalker they control, or a battle they protect (802.4a/802.4b), so a Magnetic Web requirement on another player's creature would be judged separately and only for attackers aimed at that player.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Arden can only produce {G}.

Why: Xenograft naming "Saproling" makes Deathrite Shaman a Saproling in addition to its other types; Life and Limb then makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands. So Deathrite Shaman is a land with the Forest subtype, and any land with the Forest subtype has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6] [Forest] [Life and Limb ruling #2] [Life and Limb ruling #3]. Naga Vitalist checks the types of mana a land you control could produce, so it sees {G} from Deathrite Shaman.

Deathrite Shaman's own first ability, "{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color," does not add any colors here. Determining what a permanent "could produce" looks at what an ability would produce if it resolved at that time; costs are ignored, but the ability still has to be able to resolve and produce mana [106.7] [Naga Vitalist ruling #0]. With no land cards in any graveyard the ability has no legal target, so it wouldn't resolve and wouldn't add mana [Deathrite Shaman ruling #0]. Mana of an undefined type is no mana at all [106.5]. (That ability is also a targeted, non-mana ability that uses the stack [Deathrite Shaman ruling #1].)

So tapping Naga Vitalist produces one {G} — not "any color," and not {C} unless some other land you control could make colorless mana [Naga Vitalist ruling #2]. If any land card were in any graveyard (yours or an opponent's), Deathrite Shaman's first ability could resolve and Naga Vitalist could then be tapped for any one color: {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players — the graveyard check for "any graveyard" simply covers more players at a multiplayer table.

question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
answer:
Direct answer: Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers twice (once normally, once from Panharmonicon), but only the first instance does anything — Dwarven Trader comes back once, and Staunch Shieldmate stays in the graveyard.

Why Panharmonicon applies: Mycosynth Lattice says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," so Animate Dead is an artifact Aura on the battlefield ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1] — only permanents on the battlefield become artifacts, not the spell on the stack). When determining what applies as a permanent enters, you check its characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist [614.12], [113.6h]. So Animate Dead is an artifact entering, and its own "When this Aura enters" trigger is a triggered ability of a permanent Adelyn controls — Panharmonicon affects a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities [Panharmonicon ruling #4], and it triggers an additional time.

First instance of the ability: Animate Dead is on the battlefield, so it loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Dwarven Trader to the battlefield under Adelyn's control, and attaches to Dwarven Trader [Animate Dead ruling #1]. Dwarven Trader is an artifact creature on the battlefield thanks to Mycosynth Lattice.

Second instance: Animate Dead is still on the battlefield, so it isn't a case of the ability doing nothing for that reason [Animate Dead ruling #2], but there is no longer an enchanted creature *card* in a graveyard to return — Animate Dead is attached to the Dwarven Trader permanent, and it can't be moved to or animate a different creature such as Staunch Shieldmate [Animate Dead ruling #3]. The zone-change portion simply fails to do anything because the object isn't in the zone the ability is looking for [603.6a]. The extra instance also sets up a duplicate delayed trigger for "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it," which is harmless (Dwarven Trader would just be sacrificed once, then the second trigger finds nothing).

Assumption on timing: Panharmonicon and Mycosynth Lattice are both already on the battlefield when Animate Dead resolves. If Mycosynth Lattice were not on the battlefield as Animate Dead entered, Animate Dead would be a plain (nonartifact) enchantment and Panharmonicon wouldn't apply at all — the ability would trigger just once.

Note: no March of the Machines is involved here, so Animate Dead doesn't become a creature and isn't unattached ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3]). All the rules used here are player-independent, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.611.3c: A continuous effect may be generated by the static ability of an object. Continuous effects that modify characteristics of permanents do so simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. They don’t wait until the permanent is on the battlefield and then change it. Because such effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, they are applied before determining whether the permanent will cause an ability to trigger when it enters the battlefield. A permanent with the static ability “All white creatures get +1/+1” is on the battlefield. A creature spell that would normally create a 1/1 white creature instead creates a 2/2 white creature. The creature doesn’t enter the battlefield as 1/1 and then change to 2/2.

Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows: An object’s ability that modifies how that particular object enters the battlefield functions as that object is entering the battlefield. See rule 614.12.

If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, “When [this object] enters, . . . “ or “Whenever a [type] enters, . . .” Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event.

answer_gold: Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to Dwarven Trader and triggers twice. The first trigger will return Dwarven Trader to the battlefield. The second trigger just does the same things again, so it has no relevant result.

question: Armani controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Canopy Vista]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Canopy Vista. Can Armani attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Armani can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico.

Why: Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," which is an attack restriction checked when attackers are declared (rule 508.1c). At that moment, Gaea's Liege is not yet attacking, so its characteristic-defining ability sets its power and toughness to the number of Forests Armani controls. Armani's 3 Canopy Vistas each have the land type Forest (they're nonbasic, but they do have the Forest type — see Canopy Vista ruling #0 and #1), so Gaea's Liege is 3/3 as it's declared. Power 3 is not "2 or less," so Reverence doesn't prohibit the attack. Gaea's Liege ruling #0 confirms you use the "not attacking" power and toughness when declaring it as an attacker; it only changes after declaration is complete.

After declaration, Gaea's Liege becomes 1/1, because Nico (the defending player) controls only 1 Forest (the Canopy Vista). That does not retroactively make the attack illegal — restrictions are only checked during the declare attackers step, and Reverence stops a creature from attacking, not from continuing to attack. So a 1/1 Gaea's Liege stays in combat and deals 1 damage if unblocked.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming no other effects change Forest counts between declaration and combat damage. Also, if Armani were to activate Gaea's Liege's {T} ability to make a land a Forest, note that tapping it would prevent it from attacking anyway, and that ability could be used earlier on lands Nico controls to pump it while attacking.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, Armani chooses which opponent (or which planeswalker/battle) Gaea's Liege attacks, and Reverence only protects Nico personally — per Reverence ruling #0, a creature that can't attack Nico could still attack a planeswalker Nico controls. Some multiplayer variants also limit whom you may attack based on seating (rules 801.3, 811.4, 803.1a/803.1b), which could restrict attacking Nico regardless of power.

question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
No. Suspending Charnel Serenade is not casting it, so Wildfire Eternal's trigger — which only lets you "cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost" — can't be used that way, and the special action can't be taken during the trigger's resolution anyway.

Why:
- Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, which a player may take only when they have priority [116.2f]. Special actions don't use the stack and happen immediately [405.6d], but no player has priority while Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability is resolving, so Ariel can't take it at that moment.
- Exiling a card with suspend explicitly isn't casting it [Charnel Serenade ruling #15], and the suspend static ability says "Rather than cast this card from your hand, you may pay {2}{B} and exile it with three time counters on it" [702.62a]. Wildfire Eternal's ability grants a free cast, not a free suspend, so the {2}{B} suspend cost would still have to be paid — the ability gives no help there.

What Ariel can do instead: as Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves, cast Charnel Serenade itself (a sorcery) from hand without paying its {4}{B}{B} mana cost — a sorcery may be cast this way during the declare blockers step [Wildfire Eternal ruling #0]. Note Charnel Serenade's own text then exiles it with three time counters when it resolves, so it comes back later via suspend anyway [Charnel Serenade ruling #3].

If Ariel would rather suspend it, they can do so at any other time they have priority and could begin to cast it (i.e., during their own main phase with an empty stack, since it's a sorcery) by paying {2}{B} [116.2f, Charnel Serenade ruling #10].

This works the same with two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided material is that the defending player is the controller of the attacked planeswalker or the protector of the attacked battle [Wildfire Eternal ruling #7], which doesn't change the answer.

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Brynn loses the game, Brynn's phased-out Fairgrounds Warden leaves the game with them — but Coleman's Alpha Tyrranax stays in exile permanently.

Step by step:

1. Psychic Purge deals 1 damage to Brynn, dropping Brynn to 0 life, and Brynn loses the game (an effect/damage causing loss; see [104.3e], [603.9]). Because this is a multiplayer game (three players named), the game continues after Brynn leaves [800.4a]. Abilities that trigger on a player losing the game "look back in time" and still see the objects as they were immediately before Brynn left [603.9], [603.10f].

2. When Brynn leaves, all objects Brynn owns leave the game, and phased-out permanents Brynn owns also leave the game [800.4a], [702.26k]. "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist for most purposes; Fairgrounds Warden was in that state.

3. Here's the key: a permanent "leaves the battlefield" when it moves from the battlefield to another zone, or — only if it's phased in — when it leaves the game because its owner leaves the game [Leaves the Battlefield]. Fairgrounds Warden was phased OUT, so its departure is not a "leaves the battlefield" event, and rule [702.26k] expressly says this doesn't cause zone-change abilities to trigger. The duration on Fairgrounds Warden's exile effect ("until this creature leaves the battlefield") therefore never comes up, so Alpha Tyrranax is never returned and remains exiled for the rest of the game.

4. Contrast: if Fairgrounds Warden had been phased in when Brynn left, Alpha Tyrranax would have returned to the battlefield under Coleman's control, and it would return even though Brynn's spells and abilities on the stack cease to exist, because the return is a one-shot effect that doesn't use the stack [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #0], [405.6h]. Also note Alpha Tyrranax is Coleman's card, not Brynn's, so it doesn't leave the game with Brynn; and it isn't exiled again by [800.4a] since it's already in exile.

Two-player note: in a two-player game the game would simply end when Brynn lost, so none of this cleanup would matter.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Psychic Purge resolves and its damage is what reduces Brynn to 0, with Fairgrounds Warden already phased out at that moment. If Fairgrounds Warden had phased in before Brynn left the game, Alpha Tyrranax would return to the battlefield as described above.

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
After the equip ability resolves, Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant as an Equipment and is no longer fortifying Spire Garden. Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a 2/8 (0/8 plus +2/+0) and is "modified," while Spire Garden is an ordinary untapped-or-tapped land with no indestructible.

Why:

- Bludgeon Brawl says "Each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact is an Equipment with equip {X} and 'Equipped creature gets +X/+0,' where X is that artifact's mana value." Darksteel Garrison is a noncreature artifact and a Fortification, not an Equipment, so Bludgeon Brawl applies to it. Its mana value is 2, so it gains equip {2} (two generic mana) and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0." It keeps its other types and abilities, so it is still an Artifact — Fortification — Equipment [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0].
- Darksteel Garrison isn't a creature, so nothing stops it from equipping [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3]; Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a legal creature to equip [301.5c].
- Equipping moves it: an Equipment can only be attached to one permanent, and attaching Darksteel Garrison to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant unattaches it from Spire Garden [301.5c]. Fortifications and Equipment work the same way apart from what they attach to [Darksteel Garrison ruling #2].
- Since it's legally attached to a creature, no state-based action pulls it off [301.5c, 704.5p, 801.9]. Its Fortification abilities ("Fortified land has indestructible" and the tap trigger) simply do nothing, because there is no fortified land — so Spire Garden loses indestructible and no longer triggers the +1/+1 ability when it becomes tapped [Darksteel Garrison ruling #1].
- Caelorna, Coral Tyrant now counts as modified because it is equipped [Modified].

Cautions on later events: if Bludgeon Brawl leaves the battlefield, or Darksteel Garrison somehow becomes a creature, it stops being an Equipment, becomes unattached from Caelorna, Coral Tyrant, and stays on the battlefield [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2].

Player count: none of this changes with more opponents. The only multiplayer-sensitive card here is Spire Garden, whose "enters tapped unless you have two or more opponents" clause was already settled when it entered [Spire Garden ruling #0]; it isn't re-checked now.

Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and not to Spire Garden.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can legally target Pristine Angel with Murder, and Murder will destroy it.

Why: Cephalid Snitch's ability says "Target creature loses protection from protection from black until end of turn." That is a continuous effect lasting until end of turn; it applied to Pristine Angel while Pristine Angel was tapped (and therefore had no protection at all), and it keeps applying for the rest of the turn. When Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, Pristine Angel's own ability gives it protection from artifacts and from each color again — but the Cephalid Snitch effect is still running and strips protection from black specifically. So Pristine Angel has protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green, but not from black. Murder is a black spell, so Pristine Angel is a legal target, and it will still be a legal target on resolution (608.2b).

Two side notes:
- Untapping Pristine Angel does not remove it from combat; a creature already declared as an attacker stays an attacker when tapped or untapped (506.4b). It will still deal combat damage.
- Nico casting Murder at a permanent Abel controls is a crime, since it targets a permanent an opponent controls (700.13, Crime).

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle is which opponent's permanents count for "crime," and Abel qualifies as Nico's opponent either way.

question: Adelyn controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Shifting Wall] in their graveyard. Can Adelyn activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Shifting Wall? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes, Adelyn can activate Back from the Brink's ability exiling Shifting Wall from the graveyard, but X is treated as zero, so the mana cost paid is {0} — Adelyn cannot choose a larger value — and the Shifting Wall token enters with zero +1/+1 counters, making it a 0/0 that immediately dies.

Details:
- Back from the Brink reads "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost: Create a token that's a copy of that card. Activate only as a sorcery." Shifting Wall is an artifact creature card, so it's a legal choice.
- Shifting Wall's mana cost is {X}. Because Adelyn isn't casting the card, there's no spell for which to announce a value of X; [Back from the Brink ruling #3] states that if the exiled creature card has {X} in its mana cost, X is considered to be zero. So the cost is {0} and Adelyn can't pay extra to pump it.
- Shifting Wall's "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is a replacement effect, and such abilities do apply to the token per [Back from the Brink ruling #2] and rule [707.5]. But with X = 0, it enters with no counters.
- Result: a 0/0 Wall token with defender that is put into the graveyard as a state-based action for having 0 toughness.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here involves opponents or turn order, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex controls the ability.

Why each piece works:

1. Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Alex's Control Magic (an Aura enchantment) is also an artifact on the battlefield and is therefore a legal thing to sacrifice to Krark-Clan Ironworks' ability, "Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}" ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1], [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3] confirm Auras become artifacts).

2. Boris Devilboon's cost is {2}{B}{R}, {T}. Krark-Clan Ironworks produces {C}{C} — colorless mana, which is not generic and normally can't pay {B} or {R}. But Mycosynth Lattice's third ability, "Players may spend mana as though it were mana of any color," explicitly lets even colorless mana be spent as colored mana ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0]). So the {C}{C} can pay the {B}{R}, and Alex still needs {2} generic from some other source, plus tapping Boris Devilboon.

3. Timing: activating an ability means putting it on the stack and then paying its costs, and announcements and payments can't be altered once made ([602.2], [701.2a]). Alex legally begins the activation while Alex controls Boris Devilboon (only an object's controller may activate its abilities, [602.2]). Sacrificing Control Magic happens during the payment of costs, after the ability is already on the stack.

4. Controller of the ability: "The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it" ([113.8]). Alex activated it, so Alex controls it even after Control Magic is gone, and Alex will get the 1/1 black and red Minor Demon token when it resolves. (Under Mycosynth Lattice's second ability everything in every zone is colorless, so the token, once on the battlefield, is colorless despite being defined as black and red — [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2].)

5. Side effect: once Control Magic leaves the battlefield, its control-changing effect (applied in layer 2, [613.1b]) ends, and Boris Devilboon reverts to Nico's control — tapped. That doesn't undo or change the ability already on the stack.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; only Alex, Nico, and their own permanents are involved.

question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
answer:
Evil Twin enters the battlefield under Nico's control, and Nico — not Aiden — chooses what it copies; and if Nico does choose Chronatog Totem, Evil Twin enters as a non-creature artifact named Chronatog Totem (not a 1/2 Atog creature), with Chronatog Totem's three activated abilities plus "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature."

Why:

1. Control. Gather Specimens says a creature that would enter under an opponent's control enters under Nico's control instead. Evil Twin is a creature spell, so as it would enter, that replacement effect applies. Gather Specimens' replacement effect is applied before any other effects that modify how the creature enters, including "as this enters" copy choices [Gather Specimens ruling #3]. That ruling explicitly covers this case: "If Clone would enter under an opponent's control, you choose which creature it copies as it enters under your control." Evil Twin's copy ability is the same kind of "as it enters" replacement effect, and copy choices for a permanent entering as a copy are made by the permanent's controller [707.6] — here that's Nico. So Aiden's intended choice is not binding; Nico may copy any creature on the battlefield, or copy nothing, in which case Evil Twin is a 0/0 and dies immediately [Evil Twin ruling #4].

2. What copying Chronatog Totem gives. Copiable values are only those derived from printed text, as modified by other copy effects; other effects, including type-changing effects, are not copied [707.2]. Chronatog Totem is printed as an artifact that only becomes a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature via its own {1}{U} ability. That animation is a type-changing effect and is not copied — exactly the Chimeric Staff example in [707.2]. So Nico's Evil Twin is a plain artifact named Chronatog Totem, not a creature, and it does not copy tapped status, counters, or any other non-copy effects [Evil Twin ruling #7]. Nico can pay {1}{U} to animate it into a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature, since it has the printed ability.

3. The gained ability. Evil Twin's granted ability is part of Evil Twin's copiable values [707.9a], [707.9b], [Evil Twin ruling #0]. Nico can use {U}{B}, {T} to destroy a target creature with the same name — Aiden's Chronatog Totem qualifies while it is a creature. Note the timing caveat in [Chronatog Totem ruling #0]: a permanent that becomes a creature can only use its {T} abilities if its controller has controlled it continuously since the start of their most recent turn. Since Nico's copy is not a creature this turn, that restriction doesn't bite; but if Nico animates it with {1}{U}, it becomes a creature Nico hasn't controlled since their last turn began, and then its {T} abilities are unusable this turn.

Ordering assumption: I'm assuming Gather Specimens resolved before Evil Twin was cast, as stated. Gather Specimens does not retroactively steal creatures that already entered [Gather Specimens ruling #0], so if Evil Twin had already entered before Gather Specimens resolved, it would stay Aiden's and Aiden would have made the copy choice.

Multiplayer: Gather Specimens isn't targeted and affects creatures entering under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4], so the answer is the same at a bigger table. If another opponent had also cast Gather Specimens this turn, the would-be controller picks which one applies first and the process repeats [Gather Specimens ruling #5], [Gather Specimens ruling #8] — with two opposing Gather Specimens the creature can end up back with the original player.

question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
answer:
It depends on turn order — specifically, whether Albert or Nico declares first, and in which round of mulligans Albert uses it.

Serum Powder's ability is used "any time you could mulligan," which means at the moment Albert would declare whether they're taking a mulligan [Serum Powder]. Declarations happen in order: the starting player declares first, then each other player in turn order [103.5b].

- If Nico is the starting player, Nico declares first, so by the time Albert must decide, Albert already knows Nico's declaration and can factor it in.
- If Albert is the starting player, Albert declares (and thus must decide about Serum Powder) before Nico says anything, so no, Albert won't know.

Importantly, Albert doesn't have to use Serum Powder in the first round. Rule 103.5b explicitly notes that the action "need not be in the first round of mulligans" and that other players may already have made their mulligan declarations by the time the player has the option to perform it. So Albert can keep Serum Powder for a later declaration, at which point Nico's earlier choices are known. If Albert performs the Serum Powder action, Albert then declares whether they're taking a mulligan [103.5b]. Using the ability doesn't stop Albert from also mulliganing, and the exiled cards stay exiled for the rest of the game [Serum Powder ruling #0], [Serum Powder ruling #1].

This is the two-player answer, as asked. At a multiplayer table the same declaration order applies, so Albert would know the declarations of every player who precedes them in turn order but not those after; note also that in a multiplayer game the first mulligan a player takes is free (no card put on the bottom) [103.5c], [800.6].

question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
answer:
Neither player can suspend Rift Sower while Sen Triplets' ability is in effect.

Why Nico can't: exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting, and a player may take it only if they "could begin to cast that card by putting it onto the stack" from their hand [116.2f], [702.62a]. Determining that takes into account any effect that prohibits casting the card [702.62c], [601.3], [Rift Sower ruling #0]. Sen Triplets says Nico "can't cast spells or activate abilities" this turn, so Nico could not begin to cast Rift Sower and therefore cannot use its suspend ability. (Nico also can't activate Rift Sower's mana ability from anywhere — Sen Triplets shuts off all activated abilities, including mana abilities [Sen Triplets ruling #5].)

Why Ariana can't: the suspend special action is available only to "a player who has a card with suspend in their hand" [116.2f], and suspend's first ability functions while the card is in its owner's hand [702.62a]. Rift Sower is in Nico's hand, not Ariana's. Sen Triplets grants Ariana permission to play lands and cast spells from Nico's hand — it does not grant permission to take Nico's special actions, and Sen Triplets doesn't change when spells may be cast from that hand [Sen Triplets ruling #4]. Suspending isn't casting [Rift Sower ruling #4], so that permission doesn't reach it.

So the second half of your question doesn't come up: no time counters ever get placed this turn. For completeness, if Rift Sower had already been suspended earlier (before Sen Triplets' ability resolved), the suspend triggers belong to the card's owner/controller of the exiled card — Nico — and Nico would be the one who may cast it when the last counter is removed [702.62a], [Rift Sower ruling #5]. But Sen Triplets' restriction lasts only "this turn," and it says Nico can't cast spells, so on a turn the restriction is active Nico couldn't cast it (the trigger's permission would go unused and Rift Sower would remain exiled with no time counters, no longer suspended) [Rift Sower ruling #5].

Once Sen Triplets' effect ends, Nico can suspend Rift Sower normally by paying {G} and exiling it with two time counters.

Multiplayer note: Sen Triplets' ability targets one opponent, so in a game with more than two players only Nico is restricted; other opponents can suspend cards from their own hands as usual, and Ariana's ability to play from a hand applies only to Nico's hand.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Short answer: after being turned face up, Wayward Angel is a black Frog creature, base power/toughness 1/1 but 4/4 after its own Threshold bonus, with flying, vigilance, trample, and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature." Its name is Wayward Angel and it is no longer an Angel Horror.

Why:

- Manifest puts the card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no subtypes, no abilities, and no mana cost; those are its copiable values while face down [708.2a] [701.40h], and this is applied in layer 1b [613.2b].
- Turn to Frog resolving while Wayward Angel is face down: it loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1. It keeps other card types/supertypes [Turn to Frog ruling #1].
- Turning Wayward Angel face up makes its copiable values revert to the card's normal values (Wayward Angel, {4}{W}{W}, Angel Horror, 4/4, flying, vigilance, Threshold), but Turn to Frog's effect still applies to it for the rest of the turn [708.8] [708.10].
- Because Wayward Angel's printed abilities only start to apply when it is turned face up — i.e., after Turn to Frog resolved — they are not stripped by Turn to Frog; an ability that starts applying after Turn to Frog resolves is kept [Turn to Frog ruling #3]. So flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability function.
- With seven or more cards in Ariella's graveyard, Threshold applies: +3/+3, black, trample, and the upkeep sacrifice trigger. Base 1/1 from Turn to Frog plus +3/+3 in layer 7 = 4/4 [613.1g]. For color, Turn to Frog set it blue and the later-timestamped Threshold effect makes it black only — not blue and black, and not white [Wayward Angel ruling #0].
- Subtype: Turn to Frog set the creature type to Frog and nothing later changes it, so it is a Frog, not an Angel Horror.

Timing assumption: I assumed Turn to Frog fully resolved while Wayward Angel was still face down, then Ariella turned it face up. If instead Wayward Angel were already face up when Turn to Frog resolved, Turn to Frog would strip flying, vigilance, and Threshold (its timestamp being later), leaving a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities for the turn.

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents.

answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature (a legendary land creature), and its only creature type is Ferret.

How it gets there:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself is a Swamp [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0].
2. Kormus Bell then makes all Swamps 1/1 black creatures that are still lands, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is both a land and a creature at once, affected by anything that affects either type [Kormus Bell ruling #0], [205.2b]. Kormus Bell grants no creature type at all.
3. Vastwood Zendikon, which enchants Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, makes it a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]. Because Vastwood Zendikon has the later timestamp, its 6/4 overwrites Kormus Bell's 1/1 [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #0], and it supplies the creature type Elemental.
4. Conspiracy, with Ferret chosen, says creatures you control are the chosen type, and affected creatures lose all of their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]. It can grant a creature type even to animated lands that would otherwise have none [Conspiracy ruling #1]. So the Elemental type from Vastwood Zendikon is replaced: the only creature type is Ferret.

Other characteristics are unaffected by these type changes: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth keeps its name, the supertype legendary, and its land types (including Swamp) [205.4b], [205.1b], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0]. Note Ferret is a legal creature type on the list [205.3m].

Multiplayer note: Kormus Bell animates Swamps controlled by every player [Kormus Bell ruling #1], and Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth affects every land on the battlefield, but Conspiracy only retypes creatures Ahmad controls (plus creature spells he controls and creature cards he owns elsewhere). So opponents' animated Swamps are creatures with no creature type, whether there are two players or more; the answer for Ahmad's own Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is the same at any player count.

answer_gold: It is an Elemental Ferret creature. Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, but it's dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, and waits to apply until after Vastwood Zendikon is applied. Kormus Bell is dependent on Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is applied first, then Kormus Bell. At this point Conspiracy is no longer be dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy is applied, and then Vastwood Zendikon.
